chapters.title: Chapter 880. If She’s Asking For Help, She’s Already Marked You Dangerous
paragraphs: Lily folded her arms across her chest, leaning against the corridor wall with the deliberate, relaxed posture of someone who had long ago learned that Rex’s moods were a weather system she simply had to endure.

"You disappear for most of the night... now, you emerge looking like you’ve walked through a war zone you refuse to explain, and the very first thing you demand from us is information rather than breakfast." She tilted her head, studying him with amusement. "That is very you... Rex."
’Lily’s being sarcastic right now... both of them probably... I fucking knew these two bitches heard me literally breeding Elizabeth. " Rex thought. ’Oh well... let them...’
"Breakfast isn’t going to solve the problem I’m facing," Rex said, his voice carrying the gravelly weight of his sleeplessness. "Though I wouldn’t turn it down if it appeared."
"It isn’t going to materialize out of thin air," Lily countered with a smirk. "You would actually have to ask nicely."
Rex’s lips thinned. "I have never once asked you for anything nicely, Lily."
"You wouldn’t know what to do with it if I started."
"Try me," Lily challenged.
The words were playful, but there was a spark in her eyes—that specific, dangerous light that appeared whenever she decided a conversation had become interesting enough to play with.
’Is this the reason why they act like this...?’ Rex tried to keep his cool. ’That God of Time is going to pay...’
Rex didn’t retreat. Instead, he closed the distance between them in two measured strides. The air between them seemed to thicken as he reached out, his fingers catching her chin.
His touch was unhurried, deliberate. He tilted her face upward, forcing her to meet his gaze.

In the harsh, unforgiving light of the morning, he looked at her with a rare nakedness, free from tactical calculation and the predator’s assessment. For a heartbeat, he was just a man looking at a woman.
"Lily," he said, his voice dropping to a register meant only for her ears, rough and intimate. "Would you have something waiting for me when I get back tonight? Anything you choose..."
"I trust your taste more than my own most days."

The effect was instantaneous. Lily’s breath caught audibly the telltale hitch of someone who had thrown out a challenge expecting a sparring match and instead received something devastatingly sincere.
"That’s... uh... that’s cheating," she whispered while pouting, her bravado crumbling into something softer, something vulnerable.
"I told you," Rex murmured, his thumb brushing against the edge of her jaw. "I wouldn’t know what to do with ’nice’ if I didn’t practice it."
From the periphery, Diana watched them. Her expression remained flat, but there was a flicker of something genuine in her eyes, a rare, unguarded amusement.
"You two are absolutely insufferable," she said.
Despite the insult, there was a ghost of a smile on her lips. It was the smile of someone who had stopped merely managing this household and had begun, however reluctantly, to belong to it.
Rex turned his attention to Diana. The shift in his energy was immediate and profound.

When he moved from Lily, he moved from playful intimacy to something heavier, something that carried the gravity of a pact. His gaze locked onto hers, and the temperature in the hallway seemed to drop.
"You," he said, his voice taking on a different texture. "I am about to walk into a house that still holds a version of you it doesn’t fully deserve yet."
Diana’s arms unfolded slowly. The amusement died away, replaced by the sharp, focused alertness she wore like armor.
"Huh...? You mean that fucking wimp named Theo..." she said softly, invoking the name, testing the weight of the moment. "You still really care about that guy, huh?"
"Later," Rex commanded.
The word wasn’t a dismissal; it was a promise. His eyes burned with an intensity that demanded her full presence, pulling her out of the role of observer and into the center of his orbit.
"First... come here."
Diana moved toward him without hesitation. There was no hesitation because there was no fear, only a profound, unspoken recognition of the man standing before her.

Rex reached out, taking her face in both hands. This wasn’t the casual touch he had shown Lily; this was something far more deliberate, a rare, fragile gentleness that he reserved specifically for Diana, knowing it was the only language that could pierce through her carefully constructed defenses.
When he kissed her, it was slow. It wasn’t a kiss born of hunger or desperation, but one born of necessity, a grounding ritual, a claim staked before he stepped back into the chaos.
He wanted to taste the reality of her, to remember what he was fighting to preserve before he returned to a world of shifting dimensions and divine threats.

When he finally pulled back, Diana didn’t immediately open her eyes. She kept them closed for a half second longer than necessary, savoring the fading warmth of the contact, her breathing shallow and uneven.
"I needed that," Rex said, his voice rougher than before, "before I go stand in front of a woman who is going to try to break my arm as a greeting."
Diana opened her eyes, and though her expression attempted to regain its usual composure, the flush creeping up her neck betrayed her.
"You say the least romantic things immediately after the most romantic ones," she murmured. But she didn’t step back; she remained within his space, anchored by the contact.
The moment of vulnerability evaporated instantly. Rex’s posture shifted, the tenderness hardening into something cold and tactical.
The soldier had returned.
"Diana," he said, his tone dropping into the register of command. "Aurelia Morr Nightwing...
"Everything you know about how she trains, her philosophy, and what she values above all else in a sparring partner."
Diana froze. Her eyes searched his, reassessing the conversation with the sharp intensity of someone who had expected a moment of shared intimacy and instead received a tactical briefing.
The whiplash between the man who kissed her and the commander who demanded intel was jarring.
"Aurelia," she repeated, the name carrying a weight of respect and caution.
"She offered to let me help her improve," Rex said flatly. "She made the offer publicly."
"In her world, that’s as good as a formal challenge... I intend to follow through."
Diana went still. Her mind began to work through the implications, her pupils contracting as she processed the implications of such an offer.

"Aurelia Morr Nightwing has been the Nightwing household’s primary combat instructor for twenty-two years," Diana said, her voice gaining a clinical edge. "She developed the hand-to-hand curriculum that Theo went through, that Iris went through, that every elite guard in the household has bled under."
"She is not just a teacher; she is a living weapon." Diana paused, her brow furrowing. "She does not offer to let people help her improve, Rex."
"That’s not how she operates, but... she offers to teach them."
"She offered me," Rex corrected, his gaze unblinking. "Specifically."
"I know," Diana said, and the gravity in her voice made the air between them feel heavy. "Which is exactly why you need to take this with lethal seriousness."
"Aurelia does not make that offer to people she hasn’t already assessed as worth the effort."
"If she’s asking for your help, she’s already decided you’re dangerous enough to be a threat."
Rex didn’t flinch at the assessment. If anything, it confirmed his suspicions.
He needed to know the parameters of the battlefield before he stepped onto it.
"What does she respond to?" Rex pressed, stepping closer, forcing Diana to meet the intensity of his scrutiny. "In a sparring partner..."
"What makes her acknowledge them? What is the breaking point she’s looking for?"

Diana fell silent. She retreated into the deep archives of her memory, accessing the intimate, dangerous knowledge she had gained growing up on the periphery of the Nightwing household, observing the brutal, bone-crushing training sessions that had defined her childhood.

"I know," Diana said, and the gravity in her voice made the air between them feel heavy.
"Which is exactly why you need to take this with lethal seriousness."
"Aurelia does not make that offer to people she hasn’t already assessed as worth the effort."
"If she’s asking for your help, she’s already decided you’re dangerous enough to be a threat."
Rex didn’t flinch at the assessment.
If anything, it confirmed his suspicions.
He needed to know the parameters of the battlefield before he stepped onto it.
"What does she respond to?" Rex pressed, stepping closer, forcing Diana to meet the intensity of his scrutiny.
"In a sparring partner..."
"What makes her acknowledge them?
What is the breaking point she’s looking for?"
Diana fell silent.

She retreated into the deep archives of her memory, accessing the intimate, dangerous knowledge she had gained growing up on the periphery of the Nightwing household, observing the brutal, bone-crushing training sessions that had defined her childhood.

chapters.title: Chapter 881. I’ve Kicked Her Ass Once, History Doesn’t Need To Change
paragraphs: "She responds to people who refuse to accommodate her," Diana said, her voice dropping into a conspiratorial murmur. "Most people who spar with Aurelia dance around her."
"They hold back... They soften their strikes because she is Aurelia Morr Nightwing, the household head’s daughter!"
"A woman of immense standing and someone who could shatter your ribs without breaking her stride if she weren’t consciously restraining herself."
"That accommodation makes her dull and it makes her sharp in a way she despises..."
"She doesn’t want a dance partner, Rex... but she wants someone who fights like they actually mean to hurt her."
Rex’s jaw tightened. ’I’ve kicked her ass before... the second time won’t be any different.’
The implications settled into his mind like lead. This wasn’t a request for assistance; it was a test of intent.
"Anything else?" he pressed, his eyes narrowing. "You knew her for years through Theo."
"There has to be something deeper than just tactical preference... something like... there has to be a tell."

Diana paused, her expression shifting from that of a strategist to someone offering a genuine confession. She wasn’t giving him a rehearsed answer anymore; she was searching for the truth beneath the legend.
"She likes people who stay after," Diana said finally. "The sparring itself, the technique, the blood, the broken bones—that is secondary to her."
"What matters to her is what happens when the adrenaline ebbs and the muscles begin to scream."
"She watches what you do when you’re exhausted, when you no longer have the energy to perform or maintain your pride."
"That is when she decides if she actually respects you."
"Most people flee the moment the drill ends, desperate to lick their wounds in private, but she... notices who stays to stand in the wreckage with her."
"That is useful," Rex said, already cataloging the psychological requirement.
He needed to show her not just strength, but endurance of spirit.
"I thought it might be," Diana replied.
There was a faint, unmistakable edge of pride in her voice, the satisfaction of a woman who had just handed her partner a weapon he could actually use.
"Do you know her schedule?" Rex asked, already moving past the sentimentality. His mind was already halfway to the training hall.
"On normal days, she’s in the training hall by the seventh hour," Diana said. "But after yesterday’s incident... I would guess she arrived at the sixth."
Rex turned toward the corridor window. The morning light was pale, stretching across the floor in thin, honest lines.
The day was claiming itself.
"Can you get me there without me arriving as a stranger?" he asked.
He didn’t want to walk into that den of wolves alone; he wanted the legitimacy that Diana’s presence would provide.
Diana met his gaze, her eyes fierce.
"I can get you there," she said, "but I want to come with you."
"Well, no shit, you should come," Rex agreed.

In that moment, something in Diana’s expression transformed. The guarded sentinel melted away, replaced by something warm and focused, the look of someone who had been given exactly what she wanted without having to negotiate for it.
"Lily," Diana called out, turning to her sister.
"Go," Lily said immediately.
There was no hesitation, no protest. She had already done the math, weighed the emotional cost, and decided that this was where she needed to be.
"I’ll be here when you get back."

Diana crossed the space to Lily, pulling her into an unreserved hug, the kind shared by two people who had weathered storms together and had finally found their equilibrium. They stood there for a moment, anchored to one another.
Then, Lily leaned in. Her lips brushed Diana’s ear, but her words carried enough clarity that Rex’s enhanced senses caught them effortlessly through his ambient awareness.
"You still have your night with Rex, Diana... I haven’t forgotten... so better make it count this time..."
Diana pulled back, her face flushed with a mixture of gratitude and that particular, warm embarrassment that comes from being seen so clearly in front of another person.
"Thank you," she whispered.
Lily turned her gaze to Rex. It was a silent communication, a complex web of meaning woven through her eyes that bypassed words entirely.
Rex met her stare with a single nod, an acknowledgment that required no elaboration. They understood the stakes.
They understood the unspoken promises.
"Come back for dinner," Lily commanded, addressing both of them. "If you can’t, then it’s fine anyway, hehehe~!"
"Yes," Rex said. Then, his tone sharpened with a protective edge. "And Lily, if Elizabeth wakes before I’m back, tell her where I’ve gone."
"Do not let her worry about it in silence."
"She has this infuriating habit of thinking that suffering quietly is the mature option."
Lily offered a small, knowing smirk. "I noticed that about her too. I’ll handle it."
"I know you will," Rex said, his voice final.
The preparations were complete. The target was set.

They departed the Starlight household as the morning light began to bleed across the horizon, not with the promise of a new beginning, but with the cold, harsh clarity of a day forced to confront what the night had wrought.

The city around them was caught in that peculiar, suspended animation that follows a catastrophe: the post-crisis rhythm where the world moves through the mechanical motions of assessment, triage, and the desperate human endeavor to reassemble normalcy from the rubble.
Pulverized stone and burnt magic filled the air.
As Rex and Diana moved toward the training grounds, they skirted the edge of the northern plaza. The devastation there was visceral.
Reconstruction crews were already swarming like ants over a wounded beast, their voices muffled by the distant sounds of grinding machinery and the occasional wet cough of collapsing debris.
The golem impact zones had been staked out with the distinctive assessment flags of the academy’s engineering corps, bright, jarring markers that bled color against the gray, pulverized wasteland.
Rex watched them pass, his jaw set in a hard line. The number of flags was staggering; they were far more numerous than his initial assessment of the night’s golem output had suggested.
The destruction wasn’t just surface level; it was arterial.
’How much deeper did those impacts go?’ he wondered, his inner voice cold and analytical despite the tightness in his chest. ’The energy signature wasn’t just kinetic... It was invasive...’
’The earth didn’t just break; it screamed.’
Diana walked beside him, maintaining a comfortable, functional silence. She didn’t offer platitudes about how things would get better, nor did she ask if he was alright.
She knew better. Instead, she watched the reconstruction efforts with the sharp, unblinking eye of someone who understood that survival was not about feeling better but about functioning better.

"The northern residential district took the worst of it," she said finally, her voice cutting through the ambient noise of distant jackhammers. "The structural integrity of the lower blocks is compromised beyond simple repair."

"The golem output was concentrated there," Rex replied, his gaze fixed on a particularly deep crater where the cobblestones had been fused into glass by the sheer heat of impact. "The distribution wasn’t random... It was targeted."
Diana turned her head to study him, her expression unreadable but curious. "You read the geological impact patterns quickly."
"Most wouldn’t have noticed the discrepancy between the force applied and the resulting displacement."

"The Earthen Authority’s passive awareness reads the substrate continuously," Rex explained, his voice flat and matter-of-fact. "To me, the impact patterns aren’t just holes in the ground; they are data points written into the geological record."
"The earth remembers exactly how hard it was struck."

Diana nodded slowly, accepting the explanation without question. She understood the burden of that kind of awareness the way the world became less of a place to live in and more of a series of interconnected systems to be monitored.
They continued their walk, two figures moving through a landscape of scars, their footsteps echoing against the broken bones of the city.
The Nightwing estate materialized before them as they turned onto the approach street, a looming monument of architectural intimidation. This wasn’t merely a residence; it was a fortress of legacy.

The heavy stone construction spoke of generations of survival, built with the defensive paranoia of a family that had spent centuries perfecting the art of being dangerous. The walls didn’t just stand; they loomed, scarred by history but unyielding in their purpose.

The front gate was attended by guards who moved with the economical precision of predators in repose. As Rex and Diana approached, the guard’s eyes locked onto them, his entire posture shifting into a calibrated assessment.
He recognized Diana immediately, but his gaze sharpened on Rex, weighing whether the man beside her was a guest, a threat, or an intruder.

chapters.title: Chapter 882. She Expected Delays... Well... I Don’t Do Delays
paragraphs: "Rex Rexilion," Diana intervened before the guard could find his voice, her tone clipped and absolute. "Aurelia invited him yesterday."
The assessment cycle lasted barely two seconds, a silent calculation of authority and recognition before the massive mechanisms of the gate groaned and began to part.

As they crossed the threshold into the courtyard, they found Elaris. Whether it was sheer coincidence or simply the Elaris-esque talent for appearing exactly where the atmosphere was most charged, she was already there, seated in the morning light.

She held a teacup with deceptive delicacy, her expression stripped of the formal armor she wore in public. When her eyes landed on Rex, that familiar, genuine brightening touched her features, the look of someone who had just encountered something unexpectedly refreshing in a world of tedious obligations.
"Rex Rexilion," she said, a smile playing at the corners of her mouth. "You are early."
"Aurelia made an offer," Rex replied, his voice carrying the blunt honesty of a man who had no interest in games. "I am following through."

Elaris lowered her cup, studying him over the rim with a sharp, appreciative intelligence. She wasn’t just looking at him; she was cataloguing his readiness, his intent, and the quiet intensity that seemed to radiate from him like heat from stone.
"She will be pleased," Elaris said. "She was discussing it at breakfast this morning."
"Specifically, she noted that she didn’t expect anyone to follow through before the end of the week."
"She expected me to take time," Rex said.

"She expected most people to take time," Elaris corrected, her gaze softening with a warmth that danced on the edge of something more personal than mere professional respect. "An offer like hers carries a specific social weight, a debt of confrontation."
"Most people respond by inventing delays, by waiting until the urgency has faded and the obligation feels less like a threat."
"You, however..." she paused, her eyes bright. "You are not most recipients."
Rex met her look with an easy, unforced expression, the one he reserved for Elaris, acknowledging her teasing without the need to deflect or perform discomfort.
"Is she at the training hall?" Rex asked, cutting through the pleasantries.
"Since the fifth hour," Elaris said, her tone shifting back to information. "She is instructing the household’s elite unit this morning."
"Twelve of their finest... She typically runs them through two hours of hell before she moves to individual work."
Rex’s mind immediately began to calculate: if she had been there since the fifth hour and was running two-hour drills, she would be approaching the individual sessions precisely when he arrived.
The timing was perfect. The opportunity was raw.
"Mrs. Elaris," Diana said, stepping forward with the precise register of respect owed to a family elder.
"Diana," Elaris replied warmly. "I am glad you’re here."
"Theo has been hunting for an excuse to be anywhere else this morning, and you are exactly the kind of ’anywhere else’ he requires."
Diana’s expression flickered through several rapid emotions before settling into something sharper. "Where is he?
"The garden," Elaris said, gesturing vaguely with her cup. "Pretending to read... but we both know he isn’t reading a single word."
Diana turned to Rex, her eyes betraying a conflict: the pull between her own objectives and her instinct to intervene in Theo’s avoidance. She hesitated, caught between two desires.
"Go," Rex said, his voice gentle but firm, cutting through her indecision. "I know where the training hall is."
Diana lingered for another heartbeat, weighing the cost of her absence.

"Go," Rex repeated, adding a note of reassurance that assured her he didn’t need a guardian, but then he starts to get close to her just to whisper right to her ear. "Make sure you’ll act like you’ve forgiven him because I want his hope to at least come back just for a bit."
"I still hate it..."
"You’ll get a reward..."
"Alright then..." Diana agreed right away.
With one final, complicated look, Diana turned toward the garden.
Rex didn’t wait. He turned toward the inner gate, his stride purposeful as he moved toward the rear of the estate.

Somewhere ahead, the sounds of disciplined violence, the wet slap of flesh against flesh, and the harsh breathing of elite warriors were beginning to echo through the stone corridors. He was walking into the lion’s den, and he intended to make it count.

The training hall loomed at the rear of the estate, a brutalist monument to violence. This wasn’t some gilded gymnasium for nobles to posture in; it was a dedicated facility designed with the cold, architectural investment of a family that viewed combat training as their primary survival instinct.

The walls were thick, unadorned stone, built to absorb both magical backlash and the literal impact of bodies being hurled against them. The entrance was not a door but a wide, yawning archway designed for rapid deployment, allowing warriors to stream in and out without the hesitation of ceremony.
Rex could hear the violence before he saw it. Even twenty meters away, the sounds reached him raw, rhythmic, and terrifyingly disciplined.

It wasn’t the performative clatter of soldiers showing off for an audience. These were the wet, concussive sounds of genuine training: the bone-deep thud of a gauntlet connecting with ribs, the sharp exhale of air forced from lungs by a precise strike, and the occasional, sickening crack of a wooden training weapon splintering against armor.
Aurelia wasn’t merely supervising; she was orchestrating. Her voice cut through the din, flat, commanding, devoid of cruelty but saturated with an exacting intensity that left no room for error.
She taught with the desperate investment of someone who believed that a single moment of hesitation in the field meant death.
Rex came to a halt at the mouth of the archway, his boots silent on the stone.
Iris was there.
She wasn’t on the training floor, immersed in the sweat and blood of the drills. Instead, she sat perched at the very edge of the hall’s perimeter, a solitary figure carved from shadow and stillness.
She looked like someone who had been observing the chaos not as a participant but as a witness to something she couldn’t quite touch. When Rex appeared, her head turned slowly.
She wore an expression that suggested her internal monologue had been abruptly interrupted by a sudden, tangible reality.
There was no performative pleasantry in her gaze. Instead, Rex saw something far more vulnerable: a quiet, unguarded relief.
It was the look of someone who had spent a sleepless night wrestling with ghosts and had finally seen a face that didn’t require any emotional labor to understand.
"Rex," she said, her voice barely carrying over the distant sounds of a sparring match that ended in a grunt of pain.
"Iris," he replied.

Instead of standing at attention like a stranger or a subordinate, Rex crossed the distance and sank onto the stone beside her. It was a deliberate invasion of her solitude, a statement that he wasn’t passing through but staying.
Iris’s eyes flickered with a brief, unguarded flash of surprise before she smoothed her features back into their customary calm.
"You did not have to sit," she said quietly.
"I know," Rex said, his gaze fixed on the training floor where a soldier had just been thrown into the wall with enough force to send a cloud of dust cascading from the stones. "I wanted to."
"You look like someone who has been sitting alone with her own company for longer than is healthy, and I would rather be bad company than let you continue that uninterrupted."
"You are not bad company," Iris said, the words almost lost to the wind.
"I have received different feedback from those who know me much better than you do," Rex said, a ghost of a smile touching his lips. "But I will take the compliment while it is offered."
A sound escaped her, a small, involuntary noise that was almost a laugh. It was sharp and unexpected, the first genuine crack in her composure Rex had witnessed since the funeral.
She looked startled by her own reaction, as if she had forgotten that joy was still a permissible human emotion.
Her attention drifted back to the floor. In the center of the hall, Aurelia was moving through the second half of the session.

The elite unit moved like a single organism, their movements precise and lethal. They didn’t need to think about where their feet landed or how to brace for a blow; the geography of the hall was etched into their muscle memory.
A fighter took a punishing blow to the shoulder, ribs audibly grinding under a strike, but he didn’t falter; he simply reset, his face a mask of disciplined agony.
"Is she always like this after a significant engagement?" Rex asked, watching Aurelia systematically dismantle a student’s guard with terrifying efficiency.
"When she does not know what to do with herself," Iris answered, "she teaches."
"Because teaching is something she knows how to do perfectly. And knowing how to do something is what she reaches for when everything else, when the world feels uncertain."
"That is not so different from what I do," Rex mused, his inner mind already analyzing the tactical implications of Aurelia’s movements. "I plan... Same instinct, different tool."
"I noticed," Iris said, turning her head to study him.

She wasn’t on the training floor, immersed in the sweat and blood of the drills.
Instead, she sat perched at the very edge of the hall’s perimeter, a solitary figure carved from shadow and stillness.
She looked like someone who had been observing the chaos not as a participant but as a witness to something she couldn’t quite touch.
When Rex appeared, her head turned slowly.
She wore an expression that suggested her internal monologue had been abruptly interrupted by a sudden, tangible reality.
There was no performative pleasantry in her gaze.
Instead, Rex saw something far more vulnerable: a quiet, unguarded relief.
It was the look of someone who had spent a sleepless night wrestling with ghosts and had finally seen a face that didn’t require any emotional labor to understand.
"Rex," she said, her voice barely carrying over the distant sounds of a sparring match that ended in a grunt of pain.
"Iris," he replied.
Instead of standing at attention like a stranger or a subordinate, Rex crossed the distance and sank onto the stone beside her.
It was a deliberate invasion of her solitude, a statement that he wasn’t passing through but staying.
Iris’s eyes flickered with a brief, unguarded flash of surprise before she smoothed her features back into their customary calm.
"You did not have to sit," she said quietly.
"I know," Rex said, his gaze fixed on the training floor where a soldier had just been thrown into the wall with enough force to send a cloud of dust cascading from the stones.
"I wanted to."
"You look like someone who has been sitting alone with her own company for longer than is healthy, and I would rather be bad company than let you continue that uninterrupted."
"You are not bad company," Iris said, the words almost lost to the wind.
"I have received different feedback from those who know me much better than you do," Rex said, a ghost of a smile touching his lips.
"But I will take the compliment while it is offered."
A sound escaped her, a small, involuntary noise that was almost a laugh.
It was sharp and unexpected, the first genuine crack in her composure Rex had witnessed since the funeral.
She looked startled by her own reaction, as if she had forgotten that joy was still a permissible human emotion.
Her attention drifted back to the floor.
In the center of the hall, Aurelia was moving through the second half of the session.
The elite unit moved like a single organism, their movements precise and lethal.
They didn’t need to think about where their feet landed or how to brace for a blow; the geography of the hall was etched into their muscle memory.
A fighter took a punishing blow to the shoulder, ribs audibly grinding under a strike, but he didn’t falter; he simply reset, his face a mask of disciplined agony.
"Is she always like this after a significant engagement?" Rex asked, watching Aurelia systematically dismantle a student’s guard with terrifying efficiency.
"When she does not know what to do with herself," Iris answered, "she teaches."
"Because teaching is something she knows how to do perfectly.
And knowing how to do something is what she reaches for when everything else, when the world feels uncertain."
"That is not so different from what I do," Rex mused, his inner mind already analyzing the tactical implications of Aurelia’s movements.
"I plan...
Same instinct, different tool."
"I noticed," Iris said, turning her head to study him.

chapters.title: Chapter 883. Two Nightwings That I’ll Need To Take Over And Break Begins Now...
paragraphs: Iris’s eyes were piercing, seeing past the physical imposingness to the machinery beneath. "You have not stopped since I have known you."
"Even yesterday, standing in front of a coffin, you were doing something with your hands the entire time."
"Small, constant movements. Like you were working through a problem, solving a puzzle, even while you were grieving with me."

Rex turned his head to study Iris, a flicker of genuine surprise crossing his features. Most people saw the surface, the calculated composure, and the unshakable focus, but few had the acuity to notice the restless machinery of his mind working beneath the skin.
"I was," he admitted, his voice dropping to a gravelly register. "And I won’t pretend otherwise."
"That doesn’t mean the grief wasn’t real... It just means I don’t know how to hold one truth without also holding three others."
"My mind doesn’t know how to switch off the calculus of survival just because my heart is breaking."
Iris met his gaze, her eyes reflecting a shared, weary understanding.
"I think I understand that better than most would," she said. "My entire life has been a performance of duality."
"I have spent years scanning every corner of a room, calculating exits, and measuring distances between exits and weapons, all while maintaining the flawless cadence of a social conversation."
"It is exhausting pretending that there isn’t a predator’s calculus running parallel to every polite smile."
"Then stop pretending with me," Rex said, his tone absolute. "I would rather you be exactly as tired and as calculating as you truly are than perform some hollow version of yourself for my benefit."
Iris searched his face for a long moment. Behind those pale eyes, the assassin’s mind ran its silent, lethal assessments, weighing his sincerity against his intent.

Then, something in her shoulders shifted. The rigid tension bled out of her posture, a subtle, unguarded loosening that spoke of a woman who had just been granted permission to simply exist without armor.
Rex turned his attention back to the violence unfolding on the training floor.
Aurelia was a force of nature. She didn’t move like someone who had studied combat; she moved like someone for whom violence was as natural as breathing.
Her competence was effortless, honed by decades of blood and bone. At that moment, she was working with one of the twelve, her movements precise as she corrected the student’s stance.

She didn’t just point at his arm; she grabbed it, her fingers finding the exact pressure point that forced his shoulder into the proper alignment. The student gasped as the correction landed with the brutal efficiency of a lesson learned through pain, his posture snapping into something far more lethal under her guidance.
Rex watched her, his mind cataloging every strike, every pivot, and every ounce of raw power she commanded. Then he looked back at Iris.
"Aurelia," Rex said, his voice cutting through the ambient noise of the hall. "The offer she made yesterday..."
"Is she in here?" Rex still asked something obvious because he’s trying to see if Iris would take the bait.

Iris glanced toward the center of the chaos where Aurelia was already moving to her next target, a young warrior who was already sweating through his gambeson. "She is... you can actually hear her from here.
"Well then... Will you take me to her?" Rex asked.
Iris offered him a dry, almost challenging look. "You could walk across that floor yourself, Rex."
"You don’t need a guide."

"I know I don’t need you to do it," Rex said, leaning slightly toward her. "I’m asking because I would rather have you beside me when I face her and because I think you’ve been sitting at this edge of the world long enough today."

Iris held his stare for a second longer than necessary. In that moment, the mask slipped; the crack in her composure widened, allowing a flash of something warm, something desperately human, to shine through before she forcibly pulled the shutters closed again.
She stood. Her movement had the measured, deliberate quality of someone gathering courage, the assassin’s practical acceptance of a necessary risk.
She walked to the edge of the training floor, the stone floor echoing her footsteps, and called out Aurelia’s name.
’It worked...’

The training hall seemed to hold its breath. Aurelia paused mid-instruction, her hand still hovering near a student’s ribs. She looked up, her sharp eyes cutting through the dust and sweat of the hall to find Rex standing at the entrance.

Her expression went through a rapid-fire sequence: the initial tactical read, the cold confirmation of who was standing there, and finally, a flat, genuine acknowledgment. But beneath the neutrality, Rex saw it: satisfaction.

She looked like a predator who had set a trap and watched the prey walk straight into it without hesitation. She looked like someone who had made a challenge expecting a delay, only to find a man who didn’t believe in wasting time.
"Break," Aurelia commanded her students, her voice carrying the authority of a general. "Five minutes... recover."

The elite unit dispersed, their breathing heavy, some wiping blood from split lips or grimacing as they nursed bruised ribs. Aurelia turned and strode across the training floor, her presence parting the students like water around a prow.
She stopped inches from Rex, the heat of her recent exertion rolling off her in waves. Her eyes were fierce, unblinking, and entirely focused.
He met her gaze, neither flinching nor faltering.
"You came early," Aurelia said.

Her voice wasn’t accusatory; it was simply stating a fact, delivered with the same flat neutrality she used when calling out a student’s mistake. But beneath the surface, there was a challenge, a test of his nerve.
"The offer was genuine," Rex replied, stepping further into the space where the air tasted of copper and sweat. "And I treat genuine offers with the appropriate urgency."
Aurelia’s eyes narrowed slightly, scanning him. "Most people who receive an offer from me treat it like a social formality."
"Something said in a moment of gratitude, a polite fiction they assume neither of us will follow up on."
"Yet here you are, standing in my training hall before the household has even finished breakfast."
"I do not make offers I do not intend to keep," Rex said, his voice steady as stone. "And I assumed the same courtesy applied in reverse.
"In my experience, when someone like you speaks with that kind of conviction, it isn’t a courtesy; it’s a contract."
Aurelia fell silent. She studied him with the predatory assessment of a seasoned commander who had just realized her opponent wasn’t playing by the expected rules.
She was weighing whether he was a man of his word or merely a man of dangerous assumptions.
"That is a very specific way of saying you expected me to mean it," she said, her tone sharpening.
"You bowed to me in the ruins of a broken street, in front of your own household’s gate," Rex countered.
The memory of that moment flashed between them: the dust, the blood, the humiliation of a matriarch lowering herself before a stranger. "People do not perform that kind of gesture lightly."
"Either it costs them something to say, or it doesn’t happen at all."
"Yours cost you something. I saw the calculation in your eyes even as you lowered your head."
"So no, I did not think you were speaking out of a moment’s gratitude that would evaporate with the morning dew."
A muscle jumped in Aurelia’s jaw. For a heartbeat, the training hall seemed to grow colder.

Her expression shifted not into anger, but into something far more dangerous: recognition. It was the specific settling of a warrior who has just realized she is being seen, truly seen, by someone who has not yet decided whether to trust her or kill her.
"You watch people closely," she observed, her voice dropping to a dangerous murmur.
"It is one of the few things I am reliably good at," Rex said. "I have found it useful in more situations than combat, if I am honest, which is not a confession I make to many people."
"Then why say it to me?" Aurelia challenged, stepping closer until she was well within his personal space, her presence overwhelming and physical. "Why strip away the pretense now?"

"Because you asked a direct question, and I would rather answer it than spend my energy managing you the way I manage most rooms," Rex said without blinking. "You do not strike me as someone who responds well to being managed, Aurelia."
"Iris told me something similar this morning, in her own way. And I believed her."

Aurelia’s gaze flickered momentarily toward Iris, who stood a few paces back. Iris’s face was a battlefield of conflicting emotions; she was trying desperately to maintain her assassin’s neutrality, but the faint tension in her jaw betrayed her.
A silent communication passed between the two women, a thread of shared understanding, warm and slightly amused, passing between them without a single word spoken.
The tension in the air didn’t dissipate; it simply transformed. The verbal sparring was over. The real negotiation was about to begin.
Aurelia turned her attention fully back to Rex. The commander had receded, replaced by the teacher of violence.
"The training floor is open," she said. It wasn’t an invitation; it was a declaration of terms.
Rex didn’t hesitate. He stepped past her, crossing the threshold onto the bloodstained stone of the training floor.
The hunt had begun.

chapters.title: Chapter 884. Being Useful Beats Being Seen, She Rehearsed This For Three Years
paragraphs: [Flashback]

The contract had not been signed with the pedestrian formalities mortals clung to for security. There was no parchment to yellow with age, no ink carved from oak galls, and no quill scratching across a table to seal a pact between two desperate souls.
The covenant between Celestina Von Starlight and Kaeleth, the God of Time, was forged in something far more visceral: a convergence of raw intent that pierced the divine framework.
It was binding not because of law but because the universe itself recognized the absolute, uncoerced alignment of two wills.
Celestina had been forty-three years old when she hunted him.

She had not knelt before a gilded altar. She had not wasted her breath on the sanctimonious rituals of the Apostle system, those pathetic displays of incense, spoken invocations, and gathered witnesses that served as little more than theater for the desperate.
Those ceremonies were designed for the masses: mortals begging for recognition, seeking the crumbs of divine worthiness while submitting to a god’s absolute authority.
Celestina had no interest in being worthy. She had no desire to be a chosen servant.
She wanted a transaction. And she wanted leverage.

For three years, she had been a ghost in the archives, her mind burning with the fever of obsession as she dissected the divine temporal framework. She had calculated every heartbeat of the cosmos until she found the crack in the armor: the exact hour when Kaeleth’s attention shifted from the glacial management of primary domains to his secondary observation function.
That was the moment the god became a predator, scanning the physical world for temporal anomalies, the jagged, bleeding disruptions in the timeline that demanded his attention.
Reincarnators were those anomalies. They were foreign bodies stitched into the flesh of reality, splinters of other worlds that refused to heal.
To the God of Time, they were wounds in the fabric of existence.

Standing atop the highest spire of the Seam House’s eastern tower, the wind howling like a dying beast around her, Celestina prepared to become a wound herself. Her heart hammered against her ribs, a frantic, rhythmic reminder of her mortality, but her hands remained steady.
She was gambling with a currency most could not comprehend: her own place in causality.
Using the forbidden mechanisms of her Balance Keeper designation, she began to twist her own temporal signature. It was a nauseating, violent process.
Inside her mind, it felt as though her very soul was being shredded, pulled apart by invisible hooks that sought to drag her across dimensions.
’Just a little further,’ she screamed internally, her teeth grinding until they threatened to crack. ’ Make them see me... Make him notice the infection...’

She forced her essence to mimic the jagged, wrong frequency of a reincarnator, a false note played on a cosmic instrument. She held that dissonance, that agonizing lie, until her vision blurred with blood vessels bursting in her eyes.
She pushed through the psychic agony, holding the shape of a foreign element until the universe finally blinked.
Then came the arrival.
Kaeleth did not descend from the heavens in a burst of light. He arrived as a sudden, crushing absence of reality.

The air didn’t just grow cold; it became heavy, saturated with a pressure that felt like being submerged in liquid mercury. The tower beneath her feet didn’t shake; it seemed to shudder in terror, the stone itself recognizing that something existed here that defied the linear progression of seconds and centuries.
The weight was not physical, yet it pressed against her bones with the force of an approaching avalanche, a divine gravity that demanded her knees buckle and her spirit break.
"You are not from another world."

His words did not travel through the air as sound; they reverberated through the marrow of her bones, a temporal vibration that bypassed her ears entirely. It was the voice of an ancient mechanism clicking into place, cold and absolute.
Celestina steadied her breathing, though every nerve in her body was screaming at the proximity of something so fundamentally alien.
"No," she replied, her own voice sounding thin and fragile against the cosmic weight pressing down on her.
"You fabricated the wound," he stated, the accusation carrying no emotion, only the clinical observation of a surgeon examining a tumor. "You made yourself appear as a disruption."
"I did," she admitted, forcing herself to meet the crushing pressure of his presence. "I made myself a target..."
"To get your attention."
Silence descended. It was not merely the absence of noise; it was a temporal vacuum.

Seconds stretched into minutes; minutes felt like centuries of suspended animation where the very concept of ’now’ began to dissolve. Her heart throbbed in her ears, thump-thump, thump-thump, the only clock left ticking in a world that had suddenly gone still.

"You have it," Kaeleth finally spoke, the vibration shifting from accusation to something darker, something almost predatory. "Understand this, mortal: very few have the audacity to deliberately draw my attention and leave this encounter with their sanity or their existence intact."
"Most who seek to matter to me are desperate to be seen to be acknowledged as worthy. But you?" Kaeleth laughed. "You made yourself into a problem... That is... a more interesting approach."
"I did not come here to be seen," Celestina said, her jaw tightening despite the tremor in her hands. "I came to be useful..."
"There is a fundamental difference between those two desires, though most mortals who grovel at your feet confuse them."
"Elaborate," Kaeleth commanded.

The pressure increased, a subtle tightening around her skull, as if his curiosity itself had physical mass. "Tell me what a mortal who has spent three years dissecting my schedule believes to be the distinction."
"Being seen is a plea for recognition," Celestina said, each word measured, each syllable a shield. "It is asking you to notice that I exist and then hoping you remember."
"But being useful? Being useful is offering you a reason to keep noticing long after the first moment has passed."
"Gods forget mortals who exist only as a single pleasantry in an eternal conversation."
"I did not come here for a conversation... I came to offer a solution."
She had rehearsed this for three years. She had lived this moment in her mind ten thousand times.
But as she spoke, the rehearsed script fell away, replaced by something far more dangerous: the raw, unvarnished truth of a woman who had gambled everything on a single throw of the dice.
"You have a problem, Kaeleth," she said, using his name, a transgression that would have shattered a lesser being. "The world is hemorrhaging timeline disruptions..."
"The reincarnator population has been hemorrhaging into this reality for two centuries, and the rate isn’t just increasing; it’s accelerating.
"Your observation function is drowning..."

"You’re spending more time patching holes than managing the flow. And you cannot intervene directly; the divine framework’s operational code binds your hands, preventing you from striking at individual mortals."
"Your assessment is accurate," Kaeleth said. The words felt like grinding tectonic plates.
"How accurate?" Celestina pressed, leaning into the divine pressure, her eyes blazing. "Am I merely touching the surface of your frustration, or have I pierced the core of it?"

"The frustration is deeper than your pathetic records could ever comprehend." Now, there was something new in the vibration, a crack in the divine composure. A tremor of something that sounded dangerously like rage. "Two hundred years ago, I could account for every anomaly in a single observation cycle."
"Now? The cycle cannot complete before new disruptions have already festered behind it."
"I am in the specific sense that matters to a being who defines existence through accounting for falling behind my own domain."
The admission hung between them like a guillotine blade.
"That is a dangerous confession for a god to make to a stranger," Celestina whispered.
"You already suspected it," Kaeleth countered, the pressure suddenly spiking, making her bones creak audibly. "I am not confessing; I am confirming."
"And in our arrangement, confirmation carries a price far higher than suspicion."
Celestina didn’t flinch. "Then let us discuss the price... I have a solution."
"It is not a cure; I am not naive enough to claim I can heal time, but it is a management system."
"For twelve years, I have built an organization dedicated to one purpose: identifying and eliminating reincarnators."

"In those twelve years, we have hunted down and erased forty-three of them." Her mind flashed to the blood, the screaming, the way the bodies of those who didn’t belong seemed to unravel when they died. "The mechanism works... and the blade is sharp..."
"Its only failure is its reach."
"Reach," Kaeleth repeated, the word echoing like a death knell.
"The reincarnator population is not scattered randomly like seeds in the wind," Celestina said, her voice cutting through the divine pressure like a blade through silk. "They concentrate."
"They cluster around nodes of opportunity. Aethelgard is the most dangerous among them."
The God of Time’s presence seemed to ripple at the mention of the city.

"The neutral city on the floating island is a magnet," she continued, stepping closer to the precipice of the tower, staring into the impossible void where Kaeleth’s essence resided. "It offers exactly what a foreign element craves: stability to plant roots and opportunity to exploit."
"Aethelgard has, at any given moment, between twenty and forty active reincarnators festering within its borders."

Using the forbidden mechanisms of her Balance Keeper designation, she began to twist her own temporal signature.
It was a nauseating, violent process.
Inside her mind, it felt as though her very soul was being shredded, pulled apart by invisible hooks that sought to drag her across dimensions.
’Just a little further,’ she screamed internally, her teeth grinding until they threatened to crack. ’ Make them see me...
Make him notice the infection...’
She forced her essence to mimic the jagged, wrong frequency of a reincarnator, a false note played on a cosmic instrument.
She held that dissonance, that agonizing lie, until her vision blurred with blood vessels bursting in her eyes.
She pushed through the psychic agony, holding the shape of a foreign element until the universe finally blinked.
Then came the arrival.
Kaeleth did not descend from the heavens in a burst of light.
He arrived as a sudden, crushing absence of reality.
The air didn’t just grow cold; it became heavy, saturated with a pressure that felt like being submerged in liquid mercury.
The tower beneath her feet didn’t shake; it seemed to shudder in terror, the stone itself recognizing that something existed here that defied the linear progression of seconds and centuries.
The weight was not physical, yet it pressed against her bones with the force of an approaching avalanche, a divine gravity that demanded her knees buckle and her spirit break.
"You are not from another world."
His words did not travel through the air as sound; they reverberated through the marrow of her bones, a temporal vibration that bypassed her ears entirely.
It was the voice of an ancient mechanism clicking into place, cold and absolute.
Celestina steadied her breathing, though every nerve in her body was screaming at the proximity of something so fundamentally alien.
"No," she replied, her own voice sounding thin and fragile against the cosmic weight pressing down on her.
"You fabricated the wound," he stated, the accusation carrying no emotion, only the clinical observation of a surgeon examining a tumor.
"You made yourself appear as a disruption."
"I did," she admitted, forcing herself to meet the crushing pressure of his presence.
"I made myself a target..."
"To get your attention."
Silence descended.
It was not merely the absence of noise; it was a temporal vacuum.
Seconds stretched into minutes; minutes felt like centuries of suspended animation where the very concept of ’now’ began to dissolve.
Her heart throbbed in her ears, thump-thump, thump-thump, the only clock left ticking in a world that had suddenly gone still.
"You have it," Kaeleth finally spoke, the vibration shifting from accusation to something darker, something almost predatory.
"Understand this, mortal: very few have the audacity to deliberately draw my attention and leave this encounter with their sanity or their existence intact."
"Most who seek to matter to me are desperate to be seen to be acknowledged as worthy.
But you?" Kaeleth laughed.
"You made yourself into a problem...
That is... a more interesting approach."
"I did not come here to be seen," Celestina said, her jaw tightening despite the tremor in her hands.
"I came to be useful..."
"There is a fundamental difference between those two desires, though most mortals who grovel at your feet confuse them."
"Elaborate," Kaeleth commanded.
The pressure increased, a subtle tightening around her skull, as if his curiosity itself had physical mass.
"Tell me what a mortal who has spent three years dissecting my schedule believes to be the distinction."
"Being seen is a plea for recognition," Celestina said, each word measured, each syllable a shield.
"It is asking you to notice that I exist and then hoping you remember."
"But being useful?
Being useful is offering you a reason to keep noticing long after the first moment has passed."
"Gods forget mortals who exist only as a single pleasantry in an eternal conversation."
"I did not come here for a conversation...
I came to offer a solution."
She had rehearsed this for three years.
She had lived this moment in her mind ten thousand times.
But as she spoke, the rehearsed script fell away, replaced by something far more dangerous: the raw, unvarnished truth of a woman who had gambled everything on a single throw of the dice.
"You have a problem, Kaeleth," she said, using his name, a transgression that would have shattered a lesser being.
"The world is hemorrhaging timeline disruptions..."
"The reincarnator population has been hemorrhaging into this reality for two centuries, and the rate isn’t just increasing; it’s accelerating.
"Your observation function is drowning..."
"You’re spending more time patching holes than managing the flow.
And you cannot intervene directly; the divine framework’s operational code binds your hands, preventing you from striking at individual mortals."
"Your assessment is accurate," Kaeleth said.
The words felt like grinding tectonic plates.
"How accurate?" Celestina pressed, leaning into the divine pressure, her eyes blazing.
"Am I merely touching the surface of your frustration, or have I pierced the core of it?"
"The frustration is deeper than your pathetic records could ever comprehend." Now, there was something new in the vibration, a crack in the divine composure.
A tremor of something that sounded dangerously like rage.
"Two hundred years ago, I could account for every anomaly in a single observation cycle."
"Now?
The cycle cannot complete before new disruptions have already festered behind it."
"I am in the specific sense that matters to a being who defines existence through accounting for falling behind my own domain."
The admission hung between them like a guillotine blade.
"That is a dangerous confession for a god to make to a stranger," Celestina whispered.
"You already suspected it," Kaeleth countered, the pressure suddenly spiking, making her bones creak audibly.
"I am not confessing; I am confirming."
"And in our arrangement, confirmation carries a price far higher than suspicion."
Celestina didn’t flinch.
"Then let us discuss the price...
I have a solution."
"It is not a cure; I am not naive enough to claim I can heal time, but it is a management system."
"For twelve years, I have built an organization dedicated to one purpose: identifying and eliminating reincarnators."

"In those twelve years, we have hunted down and erased forty-three of them." Her mind flashed to the blood, the screaming, the way the bodies of those who didn’t belong seemed to unravel when they died.
"The mechanism works... and the blade is sharp..."
"Its only failure is its reach."
"Reach," Kaeleth repeated, the word echoing like a death knell.
"The reincarnator population is not scattered randomly like seeds in the wind," Celestina said, her voice cutting through the divine pressure like a blade through silk.
"They concentrate."
"They cluster around nodes of opportunity.
Aethelgard is the most dangerous among them."
The God of Time’s presence seemed to ripple at the mention of the city.
"The neutral city on the floating island is a magnet," she continued, stepping closer to the precipice of the tower, staring into the impossible void where Kaeleth’s essence resided.
"It offers exactly what a foreign element craves: stability to plant roots and opportunity to exploit."
"Aethelgard has, at any given moment, between twenty and forty active reincarnators festering within its borders."

chapters.title: Chapter 885. An Efficiency That Happens To Be Cruel, Very Fine Distinction
paragraphs: "I am aware of the infection," Kaeleth said, the vibration of his voice carrying a note of weary disgust.
"My organization’s current methodology is failing against that density," Celestina said. "We operate on surgical precision: identify, profile, and eliminate."
"We kill them in the shadows, ensuring our existence remains a myth. But surgery fails when you are dealing with a tumor that has already claimed the entire organ."
"If we continue to pick off targets one by one in Aethelgard, we will inevitably trigger a coordinated response."
"The reincarnators will realize they are being hunted, they will unite, and they will burn my organization to ash."
"And the destruction of your organization would create a cascade of unmanaged anomalies," Kaeleth observed. "The wound would fester beyond repair."
"Exactly," Celestina said. "Which is why I need to stop treating them as individual targets."
"I need to treat them as a contained system."
"Speak," Kaeleth commanded. "Show me the shape of your madness."

Celestina began to speak, and as she did, her mind raced through the intricate, terrifying blueprints she had constructed over years of sleepless nights. She described the time loop architecture not as a simple circle but as a complex, multi-layered temporal cage.

She explained how she would lock Aethelgard’s entire population into a defined period, a controlled segment of time that could be managed, monitored, and, most importantly, reset at the whim of the operator.
She detailed the reset condition: a trigger tied to the Apostle network’s psychological state, a divine tripwire that would snap the loop shut the moment the variables deviated from her plan.

She described how the working would be seamless, invisible even to those trapped within it, because temporal manipulation at the foundational level does not feel like an external force; it feels like destiny.

"There is a fatal flaw in your calculus," Kaeleth interrupted, the divine weight suddenly intensifying until Celestina’s teeth began to ache. "A working of this magnitude cannot simply exist in a vacuum... It must displace reality."
"If a population’s sense of elapsed time is severed from the natural passage of days, they will notice."
"They will feel the hollow ache where their history should be."
"They will begin to ask why the sun rises but the years do not turn, and they will notice the absence."
Celestina felt a bead of sweat roll down her temple. ’Don’t break now... Not when you can taste the victory.’
"I anticipated that concern," she said, her voice steady despite the hammering in her chest. "I spent three years accounting for the perception of absence."
"Then give me your answer, mortal..."
"How do you prevent them from realizing they are living in a lie?"

"The working does not manufacture a false sense of time passing," Celestina said, her eyes narrowing as she delivered the killing blow to his doubt. "It simply removes their ability to measure it with certainty."
"There is a profound psychological difference. A man who believes six months have passed when only six weeks have passed is a man who will notice the discrepancy the moment he speaks to an outsider."
"He will see the contradiction and panic. But a man who simply cannot say how long it has been?"
"A man who reaches for a date and finds the number soft, blurred at the edges?
She watched the divine presence hesitate.
"Uncertainty about duration is not a foreign concept to mortals," she pressed on. "We lose ourselves in time constantly."
"Grief blurs the weeks... War erases the months... A prolonged crisis makes days bleed into one another without any divine hand involved..."
"I am not giving them a lie; I am giving them a fog."
"You propose to weaponize ordinary human confusion," Kaeleth murmured, the vibration shifting to something closer to respect. "You wish to make the supernatural feel mundane."
"Precisely," Celestina said. "No one in Aethelgard will stop mid-stride to demand the exact date from the sky."
"They will reach for an approximation, ’six months’ or ’nearly a year,’ and that approximation will hold because nothing in their immediate sensory experience will contradict it."
"The loop doesn’t need to convince them that time has passed; it only needs to ensure they never feel desperate enough to seek an exact answer."
"And when the desperate inevitably come looking?" Kaeleth asked, his voice dropping to a dangerous whisper. "When the scholars and the paranoid demand proof?"
"Then they will find the proof they seek," Celestina said with a cold smile. "They will find records... even journals like the academy archives with dated entries."
"The loop’s architecture will produce internally consistent documentation as a fundamental side effect."
"The calendars will align, the ledgers will balance, and the correspondence will flow in perfect chronological order."
"The paper will agree with itself, even if the paper contradicts the true number of days passing outside the radius."
"Mortals have always been more willing to trust a dated document than their own faltering memories. I am counting on that fundamental weakness."
The silence that followed was not empty; it was a pressurized chamber. Kaeleth did not respond immediately.

Instead, the divine presence seemed to withdraw slightly, not in retreat, but in calculation, the way a predator might pause to weigh the lethality of a new prey. The temporal vibrations ceased their aggressive assault, leaving Celestina standing in a ringing quiet that felt more dangerous than the storm.
"That is more sophisticated than any deception I expected from a mortal," Kaeleth finally spoke.
His voice was no longer a crushing weight but a cold, razor-sharp edge that cut through the air. "When you first approached me, you asked for a work that would go unnoticed."
"I expected a veil, a simple shroud of illusion. But you are not asking me to lie to them."
The pressure around Celestina’s temples eased just enough for her to draw a steadying breath.
"You are asking me to amputate their ability to perceive reality," he continued. "And you are asking me to remove the one tool they would need to expose the lie themselves."
"You aren’t hiding the truth; you are dismantling the compass they would use to find it."
"Yes," Celestina said, her voice gaining a harder, more clinical edge. "I have no interest in the crude mechanics of deception."
"Lying creates vulnerabilities and contradictions that must be maintained, patterns that can be spotted, and threads that can be pulled.
"A lie is a wound that requires constant tending. But removing their capacity for precise measurement? That is clean and that is... absolute."
"Nobody has to be told something false; they simply cease to be equipped to verify what is true."
"Even the reincarnators," Kaeleth said, the vibration of his voice carrying a sudden, ominous warning. "You speak as if this is a net that catches everything, but you forget their nature."
"A reincarnator’s entire existence in this world is built upon the fact that they arrived from somewhere else."
"They carry a different clock in their minds, a different rhythm in their souls."
"Their relationship to time is already fractured, already foreign... How do you plan to cage something that already exists outside of linear causality?"
Celestina felt a flicker of something not fear but the adrenaline of a gambler seeing the opponent reveal their hand. She had anticipated this.
"I am counting on that fracture, Kaeleth," she said, stepping forward until she was nearly touching the epicenter of his divine aura. "That is exactly why it will work."
"A native of this world who feels their sense of time slipping might panic and investigate. But a reincarnator...?"
"A reincarnator who feels their internal sense of duration drifting out of alignment with the world around them will not suspect a divine working."
"They will suspect themselves."
Her mind flashed to the faces of the forty-three; she had already eliminated the confusion in their eyes when they realized their powers couldn’t save them from a world that no longer made sense.

"They already live with the expectation that this world feels wrong at the edges," Celestina pressed, her words coming faster now, fueled by the conviction of three years of obsession. "They expect dissonance..."
"They expect to feel like foreign bodies in a strange anatomy."
"When the temporal fog rolls in, they won’t look to the sky for answers; they will look inward, blaming their own disorientation on the strangeness of their own nature."
"I am not inventing a new fear; I am simply cloaking my working in an expectation they already possess."
"That is cruelty dressed as efficiency," Kaeleth observed.
There was no moral outrage in his tone, no divine condemnation. It was merely the flat, terrifyingly objective observation of a scientist naming a new phenomenon.
Celestina didn’t flinch. She didn’t apologize.
"It is an efficiency that happens to be cruel."
Her inner voice screamed at the coldness of her own words, but she suppressed it with iron discipline. ’Emotions are variables, and variables create errors... Errors kill.’

"I am not going to pretend the distinction matters to the people trapped within the loop," she said aloud, meeting the void where his eyes would be. "Their suffering and their confusion will be real regardless of how I label it. But it matters to me."
"Because I would rather build something precise than something merely vicious, and precision is what I am offering you."
"I am offering you a way to fix the wound without ever having to touch the flesh."

chapters.title: Chapter 886. Which One Are You, He Asked, The Second, She Said, No Hesitation
paragraphs: The air in the tower seemed to solidify, turning from a gas to something viscous and oppressive, like breathing liquid mercury. Celestina could feel the cost of her proposal settling in her lungs.
She began to lay out the true mechanics of the slaughter, not of bodies but of causality itself.

She described how she would use the loop’s duration to plant Legion assets like poisonous seeds within Aethelgard’s power structure. She spoke of cultivating specific social and political pressures that would inevitably drive the Apostle network toward the precise psychological state required to trigger the Reset.

The end goal was not salvation; it was a controlled collapse. At the moment of maximum vulnerability, the working would reach its full expression, unraveling every achievement, every alliance, and every scrap of progress the reincarnators had clawed from this world, snapping them back to the sterile starting point she had defined.
"Not all of them will survive the reset," Kaeleth interrupted. His voice wasn’t a sound; it was a seismic shift that rattled Celestina’s ribcage. "The reset will not merely erase their progress..."
"It will erase their existence."
"No," Celestina agreed, her voice flat, stripped of all pretense.

"Those whose survival in the current timeline is contingent upon developments the reset will undo," Kaeleth continued, the divine pressure intensifying until Celestina felt a sharp, stabbing pain behind her eyes. "Their children... Their legacies... The very foundations of their lives..."
"They will be snuffed out like candles in a hurricane."
"Yes," she said.
"Say their names to me now," Kaeleth commanded.
The command was absolute, a physical force that demanded submission. "Not because I require it for my records."
"But because I want to witness the moment you confront the reality of what you are asking..."
"I want to know if you have truly considered the specific souls this mechanism will annihilate or if you have merely reduced them to convenient abstractions."
Celestina did not answer immediately. For the first time since she had stepped into this impossible space, the silence was hers.

It was not a divine pause but a human one, a moment where her mind raced through the terrifying calculus of her own ambition. A flash of memory struck her: the face of a young girl she had hunted three years ago, the way her bones had snapped like dry kindling under the pressure of a Legion operative’s strike, the wet, gurgling sound of her final breath.
That girl had been a person. In Aethelgard, there would be thousands more.
"I do not know their names yet," Celestina said finally.
Her voice was hoarse, but it did not waver. "The working has not begun, and the timeline is still fluid."
"I do not know who will be born within its radius by the time the reset condition is met..."
"I do not know which innocents will build lives that depend on a sequence of events that the loop will inevitably erase, so I am asking you to help me eliminate people I cannot currently name."
"That does not trouble you," Kaeleth said. It wasn’t an accusation; it was a diagnosis.
"It troubles me exactly as much as it should," Celestina snapped back, the fire in her blood momentarily overriding her caution. "Which is to say, it does not stop me.

"Because twelve years ago, I made a choice. I decided that the alternative, a world where the disruption continues to compound, where your observation function falls further behind the curve, where the imbalance between this reality and the infiltrators grows until the fabric of existence itself tears—that troubles me more."
"I am not asking you to make this comfortable for me, Kaeleth..."
"I am not asking for absolution... but I am asking you to make it possible."
The silence that followed was heavier than anything she had experienced. It felt as though the tower itself were holding its breath, waiting for the verdict of a god.

"You are asking me to perform a sustained temporal working on a city of forty thousand people," Kaeleth said, his voice dripping with the cold irony of eternity. "All to facilitate the elimination of twenty to forty reincarnators."

"I am asking you to perform a working that addresses the systemic threat those twenty to forty reincarnators represent," Celestina corrected, leaning into the danger. "You have been trying to solve this problem through legitimate channels for two hundred years."
"You have been playing at chess while the board itself is being eaten by termites."
"The population is growing faster than your ability to count them."
"My approach is not elegant... It is not pretty either, but... it is effective."
"What do you offer in exchange for this violation of causality?" Kaeleth asked. "What could a mortal possibly provide to a god who has seen everything?"
"My organization’s continued operation," Celestina said, her eyes locking onto the void with terrifying certainty. "Not just in Aethelgard, but everywhere..."
"The infection you see in Aethelgard exists in every major population center in this world."
"You are drowning in details, Kaeleth..."
"I am offering to be the scalpel that cleans the wound at scale, indefinitely, and... I am offering you the one thing you lack: control."

The silence that followed her offer was not merely quiet; it was a physical phenomenon. The air in the tower grew dense, charged with an ancient, terrifying energy that made the fine hairs on Celestina’s arms stand on end.

It felt as though she were standing at the epicenter of a collapsing star. Kaeleth was processing not with the linear deliberation of a human mind but with the vast, multithreaded calculation of a deity who perceived all possible futures simultaneously.
"The divine framework’s code prohibits direct intervention on behalf of individual mortals," Kaeleth said finally.
His voice didn’t just echo; it resonated through her very marrow, each syllable carrying the weight of unchangeable law. "You ask for a weapon of mass erasure, Celestina."
"You ask for a violation of the natural flow that borders on heresy."

"I am not asking you to act on my behalf," Celestina countered immediately, her voice cutting through the divine pressure like a scalpel through necrotic flesh. "I am asking you to perform a temporal management function that is fundamentally consistent with your divine mandate."
She took a step forward, refusing to let the intimidation break her stride. "The management of timeline disruptions is your domain."
"Aethelgard’s concentrated reincarnator population is not a community; it is a tumor...
"It is a concentrated, destabilizing disruption in the causality of this world."
"My proposed working does not create a new problem; it addresses an existing one."
"That interpretation is creative," Kaeleth said.
The words were laced with something dangerously close to amusement, the kind of amusement a child might show before pulling the wings off an insect.
"It is accurate," Celestina said. Her pulse was hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird, but her expression remained as cold and unyielding as marble.
"Those two things are not always the same," Kaeleth observed.

The divine aura around him flared briefly, a flash of gold and shadow that made the edges of Celestina’s vision blur. "Though I notice you have arranged your language so that they appear to be every single time you have spoken tonight."
"You describe personal favors as management functions..."
"You describe mass extermination as addressing disruptions."
"You have a remarkable talent for finding the precise architecture of a sentence that allows both of us to agree to it for entirely different reasons."

The question hung between them like a guillotine blade suspended by a single thread. Celestina didn’t blink.

She met the void with everything she had. "I am giving you language you can use with the rest of the divine community if this is ever questioned and we both know it will be."

She began to lay out the true mechanics of the slaughter, not of bodies but of causality itself.
She described how she would use the loop’s duration to plant Legion assets like poisonous seeds within Aethelgard’s power structure.
She spoke of cultivating specific social and political pressures that would inevitably drive the Apostle network toward the precise psychological state required to trigger the Reset.
The end goal was not salvation; it was a controlled collapse.

At the moment of maximum vulnerability, the working would reach its full expression, unraveling every achievement, every alliance, and every scrap of progress the reincarnators had clawed from this world, snapping them back to the sterile starting point she had defined.
"Not all of them will survive the reset," Kaeleth interrupted.
His voice wasn’t a sound; it was a seismic shift that rattled Celestina’s ribcage.

"It will erase their existence."
"No," Celestina agreed, her voice flat, stripped of all pretense.

"Those whose survival in the current timeline is contingent upon developments the reset will undo," Kaeleth continued, the divine pressure intensifying until Celestina felt a sharp, stabbing pain behind her eyes.
"Their children...
Their legacies...
The very foundations of their lives..."
"They will be snuffed out like candles in a hurricane."
"Yes," she said.
"Say their names to me now," Kaeleth commanded.
The command was absolute, a physical force that demanded submission.
"Not because I require it for my records."
"But because I want to witness the moment you confront the reality of what you are asking..."
"I want to know if you have truly considered the specific souls this mechanism will annihilate or if you have merely reduced them to convenient abstractions."

A flash of memory struck her: the face of a young girl she had hunted three years ago, the way her bones had snapped like dry kindling under the pressure of a Legion operative’s strike, the wet, gurgling sound of her final breath.
That girl had been a person.

"The working has not begun, and the timeline is still fluid."
"I do not know who will be born within its radius by the time the reset condition is met..."
"I do not know which innocents will build lives that depend on a sequence of events that the loop will inevitably erase, so I am asking you to help me eliminate people I cannot currently name."
"That does not trouble you," Kaeleth said.
It wasn’t an accusation; it was a diagnosis.
"It troubles me exactly as much as it should," Celestina snapped back, the fire in her blood momentarily overriding her caution.
"Which is to say, it does not stop me.
"Because twelve years ago, I made a choice.

The silence that followed was heavier than anything she had experienced.

"You are asking me to perform a sustained temporal working on a city of forty thousand people," Kaeleth said, his voice dripping with the cold irony of eternity.

"You have been playing at chess while the board itself is being eaten by termites."
"The population is growing faster than your ability to count them."
"My approach is not elegant...
It is not pretty either, but... it is effective."
"What do you offer in exchange for this violation of causality?" Kaeleth asked.
"What could a mortal possibly provide to a god who has seen everything?"

I am offering you the one thing you lack: control."
