chapters.title: Chapter 887. No One’s Memory Would Be Permitted To Hold A Steady Rhythm
paragraphs: The silence that followed was different. It was no longer the oppressive weight of a predator assessing prey, nor the sharp edge of a debate.
It was something far more profound: the sound of a cosmic mind recalibrating. The very fabric of reality seemed to shudder as Kaeleth shifted his assessment of the mortal standing before him.
The divine presence didn’t just observe her now; it began to weigh her as an equal variable in a grand equation.
"That is the first genuinely useful thing you have offered me tonight," Kaeleth said.
His voice had lost its mocking edge, replaced by something colder, something almost resembling respect. "Not the working itself... But the cover for it."
"You understood that I would eventually require plausible deniability, so you built the legal architecture into the proposal before I could even ask for it."
Celestina felt a tremor of triumph in her chest, though she kept her features as frozen as ice. "I told you, Kaeleth..."
"I did not come here for a single conversation, but I came here to conclude a transaction."

"The working will be inextricably tied to your operational objectives," Kaeleth warned, his aura flaring like a dying sun, casting jagged shadows across the chamber. "Understand this: if your objectives shift, if your purpose wavers or changes direction, the working’s anchor will become unstable."
"The temporal loop will fracture, and the resulting backlash could tear Aethelgard apart before the reset even begins."

"My objectives will not change," Celestina said, her voice ringing with the conviction of someone who had already burned every bridge behind her. "I have sacrificed everything my morality, my peace, my humanity to this singular purpose..."
"I am not a woman who wavers."
"They have not changed in twelve years," Kaeleth observed. "I have watched your organization’s trajectory from the periphery."
"You are consistent. That is a rare quality in your kind."
Celestina’s eyes narrowed.
"You were watching me long before tonight." It wasn’t quite a question; it was a realization that chilled her more than any divine threat.

"I watch every sustained disruption to the timeline," Kaeleth said. "An organization that eliminates reincarnators with such relentless consistency over twelve years produces a very specific, very legible pattern in the fabric of causality."

"Each elimination you make is a small stitch, a minor correction that my observation function registers automatically, whether I am paying direct attention or not. I noticed your pattern approximately four years ago."
A muscle jumped in Celestina’s jaw.
’Four years...’ She had thought she was a ghost, a shadow moving through the world unnoticed.

"I did not know it was you, specifically, standing at the center of that web," Kaeleth continued, his presence expanding until it felt as though the walls of the tower were dissolving into the void. "Until you climbed this tower tonight and made yourself visible on purpose."
"You stopped being a pattern and became a person."
"Four years," Celestina repeated.
A strange, dark satisfaction curled in her throat. "I did not expect to have been noticed that early."

"You were thorough," Kaeleth said, and there was a terrifying sincerity in his words. "Thoroughness is legible to anyone whose entire function is reading patterns, even when the thorough person believes herself to be invisible."
"You left too many clean graves, Celestina."
"Yes," she whispered. "Perhaps I left too many.
"I will do this," Kaeleth declared.
The shift in the air was instantaneous. The tension didn’t vanish; it solidified.
The divine intent settled into the environment like molten lead, heavy and irreversible. "The working begins when you are ready."
"The reset condition will be exactly as you described and the duration will remain indefinite, lasting until the condition is met or until you withdraw the anchor yourself."
Celestina took a breath, but she didn’t relax. The deal was struck, but the weapon needed to be perfect.
"There is one more thing I want confirmed before I agree to the terms."
The divine presence stilled. "Speak."

"The people inside the working during its duration, however long that may last I do not want them merely confused about elapsed time in the abstract," she said, her voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper that carried more power than a scream. "I want the confusion to be load bearing."

"I want a reincarnator standing in that city, at any point during the working’s life, to be fundamentally, biologically unable to say with confidence how long it has been since they arrived in this world..."
"Not approximately unable. Not ’I lost track of time.’ I want them to be actually unable, in a way that no conversation, no calendar, and no comparison of notes can resolve."
Kaeleth’s aura pulsed with curiosity. "Why that specific cruelty?"

"Because a reincarnator who knows exactly how long he has been building something is a reincarnator who can defend the timeline of his creation," Celestina said, her eyes blazing with cold calculation. "A reincarnator who can point to a date and say, ’I have held this position for six months,’ possesses a weapon of certainty."
"But a reincarnator who cannot say for certain whether it has been four months, six months, or eight months is a man whose entire operational history becomes soft... unverifiable... and fragile..."
"I want that softness available to me as a weapon just in case the reset condition is never met and I need another way to unmake everything they have built."

"You are already planning for the working’s failure," Kaeleth said, his voice dropping to a register that made the stone floor beneath Celestina’s boots vibrate. "You are asking me to initiate a cosmic operation while simultaneously preparing the tools to dismantle it."
"You are asking for a weapon and a shield in the same breath."

"I plan for failure in every arrangement I make," Celestina shot back, her voice unyielding despite the way her heart hammered against her ribs. "Failure is not an inconvenience; it is a statistical certainty."
"It is the specific reason my organization has survived twelve years in a world that would prefer it did not exist."
"We survive because we assume every knife at our throat is already halfway through our skin."
Kaeleth’s presence surged, a cold wave of divine inevitability. "The confusion you are describing will not be limited to your targets, Celestina..."
"You cannot surgically remove the concept of time from only certain minds without leaving scars on the fabric itself."
"If I remove the population’s ability to measure elapsed time with precision, the effect touches the foundational layer of causality, the very substrate that every soul in that city is connected to."
"Your own operatives will be drowned in it.
The god’s eyes, twin voids of ancient knowledge, bored into hers. "Valentina Von Starlight, who has led that academy for decades with ruthless precision, will find herself equally adrift."
"She will become unable to say with total confidence how long it has been since specific events occurred, even events she believes she remembers with absolute clarity."
"Her certainty will become as soft as the peasant’s."
Celestina steeled herself. A flash of doubt flickered in her mind—the image of Valentina’s face, sharp and commanding—but she crushed it.
Doubt was a luxury she had burned away years ago.
"That is acceptable," Celestina said. "Valentina has kept meticulous records for decades precisely because she does not trust her own memory over long periods."
"She has built her authority on documentation... When the fog rolls in, she will not reach for her recollection; she will reach for her ledgers."
"And those ledgers, rewritten by the very mechanics of the working, will agree with the working’s version of reality rather than the true one."
"I am not concerned about my own people being caught in the fog, but I am concerned about the fog holding."

She leaned forward, her shadow stretching long and thin across the divine chamber. "A fog that only surrounds my targets while leaving everyone else perfectly clear-eyed would not be a natural phenomenon."
"It would be an obvious anomaly, a beacon of suspicion, and it would be the one unnatural feature in an otherwise seamless confusion..."
"I want the lie to be absolute."
"You want the fog to be completely dense so that it never appears artificially created," Kaeleth mused, the realization rippling through the air like a shockwave.

"Yes," Celestina said, her voice carrying a grim satisfaction. "The moment anyone in that city can point to a single person whose sense of time is suspiciously precise while everyone else’s has eroded, they will start asking questions."
"And the questions will lead directly back to us... Total confusion is safer than selective confusion."

"It is also, I will admit, the more honest version of what I am asking for... so I would rather build one true, all-consuming fog than a hundred small, manufactured certainties that I would have to defend individually."
"That is the most honest thing you have said to me tonight," Kaeleth said.
The words felt like a benediction and a curse all at once. "This statement stands out in a conversation that has otherwise been constructed entirely out of careful phrasing and tactical obfuscation."
"I try to save the honesty for the parts that matter," Celestina replied, her mask slipping just enough to reveal the cold steel beneath. "It is more effective that way."
She had been forty-three years old when she made that bargain.
The conversation had lasted approximately twenty minutes, but the consequences would last for centuries.
The work had begun six months ago, or perhaps it had been eight. Or perhaps it had only been three weeks.

To the people inside the radius, time had become something viscous, something that could be stretched or compressed without warning. They would reach for dates, for seasons, for the passage of years, only to find their fingers slipping through something that felt like smoke.
Every dated record in Aethelgard would now agree with the working’s version of reality, a consensus of lies written in ink and stone.

No one’s actual memory would be permitted to keep an honest count because no one’s memory had been allowed to hold a steady rhythm since the night Celestina Von Starlight stood atop a lonely tower and made a foreign god notice her on purpose.

chapters.title: Chapter 888. The Prey Had Been Waiting For The Trapper To Set It
paragraphs: [Present]
The throne room was not a place of ceremony. Celestina had no subjects to impress, no nobles to intimidate, and no court to maintain.
She held no kingdom; she managed an apparatus, a complex, multi-tiered structure of operatives designed to keep her at its invisible center. The room existed for one purpose: thought.
It was a cathedral of silence, constructed from the same cold, unyielding stone that formed the Seam House itself. The throne was a slab of ancient granite positioned at the far end of the chamber.

Afternoon light bled through narrow, slit-like windows, cutting across the center of the room in sharp amber blades, but the throne itself remained swallowed in deliberate shadow. Celestina sat within that darkness, her posture perfect, the practiced stillness of a woman who had spent decades learning how to occupy space without disturbing it.
Her eyes drifted to the time crystal resting on the armrest’s built-in shelf. It was dark.

It had remained dark since Rex had returned from Ignivara, his face splattered with the dried crimson of whatever atrocity he had performed to secure the mission. He had crushed the communication crystal he’d retrieved, severing the direct channel to the field in a moment of violent finality.
But with this crystal, this was different. This was not the blue-white stutter of the operational relay network.
This was Kaeleth’s direct line. A divine frequency.
It had been dark because Kaeleth had not called. Until now.

The crystal suddenly ignited, pulsing with a deep, ominous amber gold that seemed to bleed light into the surrounding shadows. Celestina reached for it with the flat, mechanical efficiency of someone who had been cultivating a specific kind of patience for exactly this moment.
"Tell me," she said. Her voice was a scalpel: clean, precise, and devoid of emotion.
Kaeleth’s presence flooded through the crystal. It wasn’t sound; it was pressure.
It was that same terrifying weight without mass she had felt in the tower, the feeling of a predator’s gaze pressing against her skin.
"The worker’s anchor has been severed," he said. The words weren’t spoken so much as they were imposed upon reality.

"The severance was not a gradual decay; it was a catastrophic system event tied directly to his divine patron."
A pause followed, one heavy with the implication of something unprecedented.

"I cannot identify the patron from the event’s signature," Kaeleth continued, his divine tone carrying something akin to genuine irritation. "The signature was masked using a technique I have not encountered in all my eons of observation."
"Don’t tell me... it’s the presence manipulation," Celestina said immediately. The words felt like ash in her mouth.
"You know this technique," Kaeleth stated. It wasn’t a question; it was a demand for confirmation.
"I know of it," she replied, her mind racing through archived intelligence reports. "It was documented in the Legion’s assessment of high-tier reincarnator abilities."

"No," Kaeleth said, and the finality of it was chilling. "It is not."

"Collapsed," Kaeleth said. "The anchor point severance produced a cascading structural instability that the counter frequency exploited like a wedge in a crack."
"The working is no longer active in Aethelgard..."
"The loop condition has evaporated, and the reset condition is gone."
"The mechanism has been destroyed."
"And the people in the city?" Celestina asked, her mind immediately jumping to the fallout. "The operatives? The civilians? The exposure to such a sudden collapse
"They have retained everything," Kaeleth interrupted. "All memories, all developments, all physical changes that occurred during the working’s duration."
"The counter frequency was designed to preserve the timeline’s integrity while surgically removing the working architecture."
"They did not reset, and they did not lose time... They simply... woke up."
"They are no longer within a managed temporal framework..."
"They are back in the raw, unfiltered stream of causality."
Celestina closed her eyes for a fraction of a second. "He is free."
"He has been free since the anchor severance," Kaeleth said. "And in the hours since that occurred, he has not been hiding."
"He has been making specific, coordinated strategic movements that suggest he knows far more than just the existence of the working..."
"He knows about us."
The implications crashed over her like ice water. The prey had not only escaped the trap, but the prey had also been waiting for the trapper to set it.
"Tell me," Celestina said, her voice deadly quiet. "Tell me everything."

chapters.title: Chapter 889. An Absence With Razor-Sharp Boundaries, Not A Ward, An Excision
paragraphs: Kaeleth began to recount what his observation function had witnessed: a clinical dissection of a predator’s evolution.

He described Rex’s movements through the Nightwing household with terrifying precision. He spoke of the skill acquisition patterns that read as more than mere practice; they were a violent, exponential expansion of capability.

He detailed the integration of presence manipulation, and then he spoke of the second acquisition, the one that had slipped through the cracks. A secondary skill, which was fundamental and devastating, had been concealed from the divine due to the patron’s new, unknown technique.
Celestina listened, her mind a furnace of cold calculation. Each detail was a new variable in a problem that was rapidly becoming unsolvable.
"He is not merely learning to fight," Celestina said, her voice cutting through the divine static. "He is acquiring divine engagement capabilities..."
"This isn’t Reincarnator combat training; he’s not learning how to kill mortals more efficiently..."
"The Presence Manipulation is the first piece of a specific arsenal designed to operate within divine registers."
"He is learning how to wound you."
"Yes," Kaeleth said.
"He is planning to come for you," Celestina stated. It wasn’t a warning; it was a tactical inevitability.
The pause that followed was not the measured silence of a god processing data. It was something far more unsettling.
It was the stillness of an apex predator that has just heard the click of a trap snapping shut behind it.
"He is planning to," Kaeleth said at last. "Yes."
Celestina leaned forward, her eyes narrowing. "You do not sound like a god who considers that an idle threat."
"I do not consider anything about this reincarnator to be idle," Kaeleth snapped.

The temporal vibration beneath his words carried a timbre. Celestina had never heard, in twelve years of contact, a raw, grinding tension that made the stone beneath her throne tremble. "I want to tell you something, Celestina."
"I am not saying this to alarm you... I do not waste energy on unnecessary alarm."
"I am saying it because you hired me to help you manage a threat, and I am no longer certain I fully understand the nature of the enemy we are facing."
The shift in Celestina’s posture was immediate. Her spine straightened, and her breathing became shallow and controlled.
When the expert admits he is blind, the student must prepare for the dark. "Explain."

"My domain’s function includes the ability to observe a mortal’s temporal thread," Kaeleth began, his voice growing distant as he delved into the mechanics of his own failure. "Not their future, which is a chaos even I cannot fully map, but their past."
"The specific sequence of moments that forged the person standing before me now."

"For every reincarnator I have observed across two millennia, that thread has two distinct segments: the foreign sequence from their original world, a disconnected, alien string, and the native sequence from the moment they arrived here."
"And Rex’s thread?" Celestina asked.

"Rex’s thread has three segments," Kaeleth said, and there was a tremor in the divine frequency. "Somewhere between the foreign sequence and his arrival in this world, there is a section that defies categorization."
"It does not read as absent, which would simply imply a void where nothing happened..."
"It reads as obscured... Deliberately, surgically obscured in a way that no natural reincarnator arrival sequence could ever produce."
Celestina sat in silence, processing the impossibility of the statement. Her inner mind replayed every file she had on Rex Rexilion, searching for the crack, the wound, and the lie.
"Obscured by what?"
"I do not know," Kaeleth admitted, and the admission felt like a crack in the foundation of the world. "That is the horror of it."
"I have spent two thousand years being the entity who knows... Even when the truth is blood-soaked or blasphemous, I see it."
"I see the shape of every sin and every miracle. But when I looked at his thread, there was a piece of it I simply could not see."
"I cannot tell if something is actively hiding it from me or if something occurred there that exists entirely outside the categories my divine perception was built to recognize."

Celestina’s voice was slow, each word deliberate as she dragged the implication into the light. "You are telling me that a reincarnator entered this world with a portion of his own history already sealed against a god whose entire existence is built upon reading history."
"Yes."
"That has never happened before."
"Not in two thousand years," Kaeleth confirmed. "I have seen Apostles with protective wards over sensitive moments their patrons wish to keep private."
"But even then, I can see the shape of the protection... I can see the outline of what is being hidden. This is different."
"This is not a ward placed over a moment, but this is an absence with razor-sharp boundaries."
"A piece of his thread that has been excised... the front and back edges are clean, as though something reached into the fabric of his soul and cut it out."
"Excised," Celestina whispered.
"Or replaced," Kaeleth said. "I genuinely do not know which, and that uncertainty troubles me more than any threat I have faced."
"I built the counter frequency he used against my working through years of patient study of exactly this kind of temporal gap..."
"And yet, his patron found a seam in my architecture that should have been impossible to locate without intimate, pre-existing knowledge of how my workings are constructed."

"That is not the behavior of a minor deity managing a new puppet... but that is the behavior of something that has done this before, something that has dismantled workings far older, far more sophisticated, and far more dangerous than the one I built for you."

Celestina absorbed the revelation in a silence so profound it felt like the throne room itself had been hollowed out. The amber light from the crystal cast elongated, skeletal shadows across her face, making her features appear as carved from something colder than stone.
She didn’t flinch; she didn’t gasp; she simply existed in the space between the impossible truth and the tactical reality it created.
The silence stretched, becoming a physical pressure, until Kaeleth broke it, his voice carrying a rare, unguarded vulnerability that made the divine frequency waver.
"I am not telling you to abandon the plan," he said, the words cutting through the stillness like a blade. "I am telling you what I am actually afraid of."
"You asked for my help as a partner, not as a tool, Celestina."
"And a partner who withholds the true depth of his assessment out of pride is a liability, a liability you cannot afford."
"I am afraid that we have spent months treating Rex Rexilion as a difficult reincarnator when he may be something entirely different wearing the shape of one."

"I am afraid that the portion of his history I cannot see contains the exact blueprint for my downfall and that whatever lurks in that gap is older, hungrier, and more dangerous than either of us has dared to imagine."
Celestina finally raised her gaze, her eyes locking onto the pulsing light of the crystal. "You are a god who has existed for two thousand years, Kaeleth."
"You have witnessed the rise and fall of empires and the birth of pantheons, but now... you are telling me you are afraid of a mortal."

"I am telling you I am afraid of what I cannot read," Kaeleth corrected sharply, his voice regaining its terrifying authority. "Those are not the same statement, though I understand why your mortal mind would conflate them."
"I am not afraid of Rex Rexilion the way a human fears a rival or a predator, but I am afraid the way an architect fears a flaw in a foundation that shouldn’t exist."

"I am afraid in the same way an accountant fears a ledger that refuses to balance, as an unbalanced ledger indicates either a fatal error by the accountant or that someone has tampered with the system."
The divine vibration beneath his words grew more intense. "In two thousand years of keeping this particular ledger, I have never once found an entry I could not trace."
"Every sin, every miracle, every twisted thread of fate has had a source..."
"Until him... Until he walked into my domain and presented me with a void I could not fill."
Celestina sat motionless in the dying amber light, her mind working with the cold, relentless efficiency of a siege engine. She wasn’t thinking about fear; she was thinking about countermeasures.
She was thinking about the blood that would need to be spilled to reassert control over a reality that was beginning to slip through her fingers.
"You need to move first," she said. The words were quiet, but they carried the absolute finality of a death sentence.
"My operational options within the divine framework’s code are severely compromised," Kaeleth warned, his voice growing grim. "The violation of my working was noted by the other gods."
"Their eyes are on me now... Direct action, divine intervention, and celestial wrath are off the table."
"I cannot touch him directly without triggering a cascade of divine scrutiny that would expose everything we have built..."
"I am paralyzed, Celestina. For an indefinite period, I can only watch."
Celestina’s lips thinned into a hard, merciless line. The shadows in the room seemed to deepen around her, as if the darkness itself were acknowledging her intent.
"Then we do not use divine action," she said, her voice dropping to a lethal whisper. "We use an apostle."

"I am not afraid of Rex Rexilion the way a human fears a rival or a predator, but I am afraid the way an architect fears a flaw in a foundation that shouldn’t exist."

"I am afraid in the same way an accountant fears a ledger that refuses to balance, as an unbalanced ledger indicates either a fatal error by the accountant or that someone has tampered with the system."
The divine vibration beneath his words grew more intense.
"In two thousand years of keeping this particular ledger, I have never once found an entry I could not trace."
"Every sin, every miracle, every twisted thread of fate has had a source..."
"Until him...
Until he walked into my domain and presented me with a void I could not fill."
Celestina sat motionless in the dying amber light, her mind working with the cold, relentless efficiency of a siege engine.
She wasn’t thinking about fear; she was thinking about countermeasures.
She was thinking about the blood that would need to be spilled to reassert control over a reality that was beginning to slip through her fingers.
"You need to move first," she said.
The words were quiet, but they carried the absolute finality of a death sentence.
"My operational options within the divine framework’s code are severely compromised," Kaeleth warned, his voice growing grim.
"The violation of my working was noted by the other gods."
"Their eyes are on me now...
Direct action, divine intervention, and celestial wrath are off the table."
"I cannot touch him directly without triggering a cascade of divine scrutiny that would expose everything we have built..."
"I am paralyzed, Celestina.
For an indefinite period, I can only watch."
Celestina’s lips thinned into a hard, merciless line.
The shadows in the room seemed to deepen around her, as if the darkness itself were acknowledging her intent.
"Then we do not use divine action," she said, her voice dropping to a lethal whisper.
"We use an apostle."

chapters.title: Chapter 890. He’s A Knife In The Dark, Also Fully Disposable
paragraphs: Kaeleth fell silent, the weight of Celestina’s suggestion hanging between them like a guillotine blade suspended by a fraying rope. The air in the throne room grew frigid, charged with the static of divine implications.

"You have been without an apostle for eighteen years," Celestina said, her voice cutting through the stillness with clinical detachment. "Your last three all died in circumstances that the temporal domain’s operational requirements produced sacrifices to the very mechanics of your power."
"Since then, you have been using our contract arrangement as a convenient substitute for the Apostle relationship. But a contract is a transaction; an apostle is a weapon."
"Apostle selection requires more than mere utility, Celestina... It requires the mortal to be suitable to be a vessel capable of containing the strain without shattering," Kaeleth warned.
"I know exactly who is suitable," she countered.
Kaeleth turned his gaze toward her, his eyes burning with a cold, ancient fire. "Given what I have just revealed to you, I need to be certain you grasp the magnitude of what you are proposing."
"You are suggesting we deploy a mid-tier reincarnator... a boy carrying a divine designation he cannot comprehend against something whose very essence defies my perception."
"If the gap in Rex’s thread means what I fear it might mean, the boy will not merely fail."
"He will not even register as a threat worth Rex’s full attention before he is torn apart."
"I understand the risk," Celestina said, and in that moment, her voice sounded less like a ruler and more like an executioner. "I am proposing it anyway. Because the alternative is stagnation."
"Every week we hesitate, Rex consolidates his position on that island, building a fortress of influence that becomes harder to breach with every passing sunset."
"You told me yourself your options are paralyzed... Mine are not unlimited, but they are not this restricted."
"Theo Morr Nightwing is a resource I am willing to spend on incomplete information because incomplete information is the only currency we have left."
"Waiting for certainty means waiting for Rex Rexilion to decide the terms of our next conversation... I prefer we set them."
Kaeleth stared at her, a flicker of something resembling grim respect crossing his features. "That is a colder calculation than most mortals make about a person they are sending to their death."

"I built an organization on cold calculations," Celestina snapped, the steel in her voice hardening. "It is the only reason we have survived twelve years against enemies who would see us burned to ash."
"I am not going to start softening the arithmetic now simply because the target has become more frightening than anticipated."
"The Nightwing boy," Kaeleth said, testing the name.
"Theo Morr Nightwing," Celestina corrected. "Reincarnator... Mid-tier system non-combat class."

"That makes him perfect: he is exactly the kind of reincarnator who can be elevated significantly through an Apostle blessing without that elevation creating an independent power base that could threaten you later."
"His history with Rex is documented: public assault, a forced apology under household pressure, and simmering, unspoken resentment."
"He hasn’t reconciled with Rex Rexilion... He is merely performing the ritual of reconciliation."
"Reincarnators are the variable that breaks the equation," Kaeleth muttered, his mind already spiraling through the tactical implications. "Designating one as my Apostle is--
"A pragmatic decision," Celestina interrupted. "You are not endorsing reincarnators as a category."
"You are using one specific tool to excise the most significant threat you have encountered in two centuries."
"And the tool will need to be disposed of afterward," Kaeleth said flatly.
"I know," Celestina replied without hesitation. "That is not a problem."

Kaeleth closed his eyes, mentally cataloguing the lethal parameters of the blessing he would have to bestow. "The Apostle designation for the temporal domain provides specific, devastating abilities."
"Enhanced time perception. Limited temporal acceleration and deceleration at a local scale. And most importantly, the Temporal Strike."
"A capability that operates at the soul level rather than the biological level."
Celestina’s eyes gleamed with predatory interest. "Which Rex Rexilion’s Infinite Regeneration cannot address."
"Correct," Kaeleth said. "The Temporal Strike bypasses biological healing because it does not damage the flesh."
"It does not break bones or sever arteries; it severs the temporal anchor that binds the soul to the physical timeline."
"Kill the anchor," Celestina whispered, the concept tasting like copper on her tongue, "and the soul loses its connection to the body."

"Death that cannot be healed," Kaeleth confirmed, his voice dropping to a funereal register. "The body may remain intact, the wounds may be nonexistent, but the soul becomes a ghost in its own machine, no longer connected to the timeline in which the body exists."
"The body dies because the inhabitant has been erased from its present."
Celestina leaned forward, the tension in the room reaching a breaking point. "Will that work on him?"
"Given what you said about the gap in his thread?"
"If part of his history exists outside the categories your function was built to read, is there a chance his soul’s temporal anchor is equally alien?"
"What if the strike finds nothing to sever because his connection to time is not what we understand it to be?"

Kaeleth fell into a silence that was not merely quiet; it was a void. Even through the limited, flickering transmission of the crystal, the pause felt agonizingly elongated, as if the god himself were momentarily suspended between two heartbeats.
The divine frequency wavered, crackling with the static of a predator recognizing its own vulnerability.
"I do not know," Kaeleth finally said, the words landing like stones dropped into a deep well. "I want to answer that with absolute certainty because uncertainty is a poison to my nature."
"I am the keeper of threads; I do not operate in the fog..."
"Yet, in this single conversation, I have handed you more uncertainty than I have provided in the twelve years since our pact began."
He paused, his voice gaining a grim, analytical edge. "What I can tell you is this: every soul I have ever measured, mortal, divine, or otherwise, possesses a temporal anchor of some description.
"To exist within a timeline is to be moored to it; without an anchor, one simply drifts into the nonexistence of the void."

"I have no evidence that Rex’s anchor is anything other than standard. And I must also confess..." His voice dropped to a whisper that carried more menace than a scream. "Until six hours ago, I had no evidence that a working of this magnitude could be destabilized by a single severance."
"I believed my architecture was absolute... I was wrong."
"So we are not just planning an assassination," Celestina said, her eyes reflecting the amber glow like twin coals. "We are conducting an experiment."
"We are testing the limits of reality itself," Kaeleth agreed, the admission tasting like ash. "I cannot offer you a plan that does not involve this gamble."
"The alternative is inaction, and we have already established the catastrophic price of standing still while he builds his empire."
Celestina straightened, her fingers curling around the armrest of her throne. The motion was precise, almost mechanical.
"Then we deploy the variable... Give it to Theo."
"The boy is unprepared for the spiritual backlash alone," Kaeleth warned.
"He doesn’t need to be prepared; he needs to be close," Celestina countered. "Let him approach Rex through the facade of reconciliation he is already maintaining."
"The Nightwing household’s fragile truce with Rex Rexilion provides exactly what an apostle requires: proximity without suspicion."
"Theo has access to Rex’s inner circle access that Rex would never grant to anyone he recognized as a legitimate threat."
"He will be the knife in the dark that Rex never sees coming because he is too busy looking at the horizon."
"And when the strike lands?" Kaeleth asked. "When Rex Rexilion dies?"

"Then the Aethelgard operation continues through conventional means," Celestina said, her voice devoid of any sentimentality. "Without his system, without the protection of whatever unknown patron lurks behind that gap in his history, and without the specific capabilities that allowed him to fracture our loop architecture, the city’s reincarnator population becomes manageable again."
"He becomes another problem for the Legion to solve with standard brutality."
"And the boy?" Kaeleth pressed, his gaze searching hers for any flicker of human mercy. "The tool that delivers the blow?"
Celestina turned her face toward the window, looking out over her domain with the cold, unblinking stare of a statue.
"He is a reincarnator," she said simply. "And our organization was founded on the principle that reincarnators are anomalies to be controlled, not allies to be cherished."
"Once he has served his purpose and the anchor is severed and the threat is excised, he will be addressed like any other reincarnator..."
"He will be processed and he..."
"...will be contained."

chapters.title: Chapter 891. ’I May Not Be Able To Help You Twice,’ That’s Words A God Doesn’t Say
paragraphs: Kaeleth fell into a silence that seemed to drain the very color from the transmission. For a moment, the only sound was the faint, rhythmic hum of the crystal, a sound that felt unnaturally loud in the wake of their conversation.
When he finally spoke, his voice had lost its divine cadence, replaced by something colder, something that sounded like the grinding of tectonic plates.
"I will designate the Nightwing boy," he said, the words carrying the weight of a death warrant. "The designation will be delivered through the standard Apostle channel..."
"He will receive the blessing, and with it, the specific, devastating capabilities I described. But there will be no briefing..."
"There will be no manual... He will not know the true nature of the weapon he carries unless he encounters a situation that forces the power to manifest."
"He will know he is stronger," Celestina observed, her mind already mapping out the boy’s inevitable trajectory. "That is all he needs to know to maintain the facade."
"Yes," Kaeleth agreed. "He will feel the surge of the designation’s power coursing through his veins, and he will mistake it for his own evolution."
"He will believe his system has simply broken through a new ceiling, and that is the standard experience for an early-stage apostle: the delusion of self-made strength."
"Good," Celestina said, a ghost of a smile touching her lips, a smile that held no warmth. "The deception is the most vital component."
"He must approach Rex believing he is merely an improved version of himself..."
"He cannot approach Rex as a weapon pointed at a target, because Rex would recognize the shape of the blade before it ever swung."
"He must be the dagger hidden inside the glove."

"This will not be instantaneous," Kaeleth warned, his image flickering as if the strain of the decision was affecting his connection to the mortal plane. "The delivery of a divine designation requires precise metaphysical conditions."
"I cannot simply force the blessing into a sleeping mind like water into a vessel..."
"The mortal’s consciousness must be in a receptive state, a vulnerability that exists between the layers of waking and dreaming."
"He sleeps," Celestina said flatly. "The boy is young; exhaustion is his constant companion."

"Not just any sleep," Kaeleth corrected, his eyes narrowing behind the crystal’s glow. "It must be the kind of sleep that occurs when the mind is desperate, searching for something in the darkness that it could never find in the light of day."
"A sleep born of longing or resentment..."
"Theo Morr Nightwing, based on every thread I have observed, is exactly that kind of person."
"He sleeps with a hunger that makes his soul vulnerable to intrusion."
"Then he is ready," Celestina said.
"The designation will find him," Kaeleth promised. "Like a predator finding a scent in the wind.
The transmission began to waver. The amber light dimmed, fading into a sickly, bruised purple as the connection strained under the gravity of what had been set in motion.
In that dying light, Celestina felt something shift. It wasn’t quite hesitation; she had long since burned that human weakness out of herself, and it wasn’t quite dread.
It was something else, something colder: a recognition that they had just stepped off the edge of a cliff and were now simply waiting to see if they would fly or shatter.
For the first time in twelve years of partnership, the silence between them felt wrong. It felt like the breath held before a scream.
Just as the light began to fail entirely, Kaeleth’s voice cut through the fading static one last time, sharp as a guillotine blade.
"One more thing."
"Say it," Celestina commanded, her voice cracking like a whip across the empty throne room.
The words were sharp, but beneath them lay a rare, almost imperceptible tension, the kind that precedes a storm that levels cities.
Kaeleth’s image in the crystal wavered, his ancient features twisted into something resembling pity.

"If the boy fails," he began, each word dripping with the finality of a funeral dirge, "and the gap in Rex Rexilion’s thread proves to be what my darkest suspicions suggest, if that void is not a wound but a doorway, then you must understand something."
"I may not be able to help you a second time."
Celestina’s grip tightened on her armrest, but she remained motionless.

"This is not a threat, nor is it a lack of willingness," Kaeleth continued, his voice dropping to a gravelly whisper that seemed to vibrate through the crystal itself. "It is a warning of metaphysical exhaustion."
"Whatever force produced that gap in Rex’s history may already understand the architecture of my workings intimately enough to counter the next attempt before it even manifests..."
"I have given you my best effort tonight in describing the risk, so I am not certain my best effort will be enough to save you."
"And Celestina... I have not spoken those words about anything in longer than either of us has been alive."
The weight of that admission filled the room like toxic gas. The implications were staggering: they were gambling not just a boy’s life, but the last viable weapon in their arsenal.
"I understand," Celestina said. Her voice was steady, but her pulse hammered against the hollow of her throat.
"Do you?" Kaeleth challenged. His eyes pierced through the transmission, searching her soul through the amber glow. "I am not asking to insult you."

"I am asking because I need to know if I am speaking to a commander who has truly heard the tactical reality of this gamble or if I am speaking to a woman who has already decided the plan is settled and is simply waiting for me to finish my performance.
Celestina stared into the crystal. For several seconds, she did not breathe.
She looked at the flickering image of the god, seeing not a partner but a mirror reflecting the terrifying precipice they both stood upon.
"I have heard every word," she finally said, her voice regaining its iron edge. "Every syllable of your warning."
"And I am proceeding anyway... Because thirty years of my life, thirty years of blood, betrayal, and meticulous construction are built into what happens next."

"The alternative you describe to wait, to gather more intelligence, to hope that the gap in his history resolves itself into something less frightening before we strike, is not an alternative. It is suicide."
"In a world where Rex Rexilion grows stronger with every heartbeat he spends alone, waiting is merely choosing a slower way to die..."
"I would rather move against an uncertainty I understand imperfectly than wait for a certainty that may never arrive."
"That is either courage," Kaeleth said, his voice fading as the connection began to fracture, "or the specific kind of stubbornness that only looks like courage from the outside."
"I have not decided which you are, Celestina, even after twelve years."
"Neither have I," Celestina replied, her gaze unblinking. "I stopped trying to decide what I am a long time ago. It does not change what I must do next."
The crystal’s amber gold light shuddered violently before dimming into a cold, dead black. The silence that rushed in to fill the void was deafening.

Celestina set the artifact back onto its shelf with a precise, controlled motion and sank back into her throne. The afternoon light of the throne room spilled across her features, casting long, sharp shadows that made her look as ancient as the god she had just dismissed.
Her expression was flat and clear. The expression of a mathematician who had reached the end of a brutal thousand-page calculation and found that the result, however grim, was workable.
She was not afraid.
Fear was a luxury for those who still had options. She had been afraid once approximately fifteen years ago when she had first understood the true consequences of failure.

She remembered the cold sweat, the way her hands had trembled when she realized that the organization she had bled to build could be unmade in a single afternoon. But she had learned to dissect fear the way she dissected everything else: by turning it into data, by making plans to counter it, and by ensuring those plans were as adequate as humanly possible.
Whether these plans were adequate for Rex Rexilion was a question that could not be answered with logic or strategy. It could only be answered with blood.
She would find out.

"Do you?" Kaeleth challenged.
His eyes pierced through the transmission, searching her soul through the amber glow.
"I am not asking to insult you."

"I am asking because I need to know if I am speaking to a commander who has truly heard the tactical reality of this gamble or if I am speaking to a woman who has already decided the plan is settled and is simply waiting for me to finish my performance.
Celestina stared into the crystal.
For several seconds, she did not breathe.
She looked at the flickering image of the god, seeing not a partner but a mirror reflecting the terrifying precipice they both stood upon.
"I have heard every word," she finally said, her voice regaining its iron edge.
"Every syllable of your warning."
"And I am proceeding anyway...
Because thirty years of my life, thirty years of blood, betrayal, and meticulous construction are built into what happens next."
"The alternative you describe to wait, to gather more intelligence, to hope that the gap in his history resolves itself into something less frightening before we strike, is not an alternative.
It is suicide."
"In a world where Rex Rexilion grows stronger with every heartbeat he spends alone, waiting is merely choosing a slower way to die..."
"I would rather move against an uncertainty I understand imperfectly than wait for a certainty that may never arrive."
"That is either courage," Kaeleth said, his voice fading as the connection began to fracture, "or the specific kind of stubbornness that only looks like courage from the outside."
"I have not decided which you are, Celestina, even after twelve years."
"Neither have I," Celestina replied, her gaze unblinking.
"I stopped trying to decide what I am a long time ago.
It does not change what I must do next."
The crystal’s amber gold light shuddered violently before dimming into a cold, dead black.
The silence that rushed in to fill the void was deafening.
Celestina set the artifact back onto its shelf with a precise, controlled motion and sank back into her throne.
The afternoon light of the throne room spilled across her features, casting long, sharp shadows that made her look as ancient as the god she had just dismissed.
Her expression was flat and clear.
The expression of a mathematician who had reached the end of a brutal thousand-page calculation and found that the result, however grim, was workable.
She was not afraid.
Fear was a luxury for those who still had options.
She had been afraid once approximately fifteen years ago when she had first understood the true consequences of failure.
She remembered the cold sweat, the way her hands had trembled when she realized that the organization she had bled to build could be unmade in a single afternoon.
But she had learned to dissect fear the way she dissected everything else: by turning it into data, by making plans to counter it, and by ensuring those plans were as adequate as humanly possible.
Whether these plans were adequate for Rex Rexilion was a question that could not be answered with logic or strategy.
It could only be answered with blood.
She would find out.

chapters.title: Chapter 892. For An Old Woman Like Her... She Got A Good Crash-Out!
paragraphs: The moment the crystal went dark, the silence of the throne room didn’t just return; it suffocated her.

Celestina remained motionless for three heartbeats, her spine rigid against the throne, her fingers still curled around the armrest. But beneath the practiced veneer of the unshakable commander, something was hemorrhaging.
The calculation she had performed wasn’t just workable; it was terrifying. It was a tightrope walk over an abyss that had no bottom.
A muscle in her jaw twitched. Then another.

When she stood, she didn’t walk; she stormed. The heavy silk of her robes hissed against the marble floor like a disturbed viper as she retreated from the throne room, her boots striking the stone with each step like hammer blows.
Her breathing was shallow, each inhalation feeling like she was swallowing broken glass.
The moment her private sanctum’s heavy obsidian doors slammed shut behind her, the dam broke.
"Fuck!" The scream tore from her throat, raw and uncharacteristic, echoing off the vaulted ceilings. "FUCK EVERYTHING ABOUT THIS!"
She didn’t stop. She couldn’t stop.

The frustration was a physical thing now, a molten pressure building behind her eyes, screaming to be released. Her first strike was aimed at the mahogany desk, a relic of ancient craftsmanship that had survived centuries of war.
Her fist connected with the wood with a wet, bone-jarring crack. Splinters flew like shrapnel, slicing into her skin, but she didn’t feel it.
The pain was distant, drowned out by the roaring in her ears.

"We’re gambling everything!" she shrieked at the empty air, her voice cracking with venom. "Everything I’ve built, everything I’ve sacrificed, thrown into the hands of a boy who doesn’t even know he’s holding a detonator!"
She spun around, her boot connecting with a priceless crystal vase. It didn’t just break; it exploded under the force of her rage, sending shards skittering across the floor like glittering teeth.
But it wasn’t enough. The anger needed more space, and it needed more destruction.
Her hands began to glow not with the controlled, elegant light she used in council meetings but with a volatile, sickly violet aura. Raw, unfiltered magical energy leaked from her fingertips.
"Is this what you want, Kaeleth!?" she roared at the ceiling, her eyes wild and bloodshot. "Is this the uncertainty you wanted to warn me about!?"
With a guttural snarl, she thrust her palms forward. A wave of concussive magical force erupted from her, striking the bookshelf opposite her.

The ancient leather-bound tomes didn’t just fall; they were pulverized, their pages shredded into confetti by the sheer pressure of her energy. The shelves themselves groaned and buckled, splintering as if struck by a siege engine.
CRACK BOOM.

A bolt of violet lightning arced from her fingertips, striking a marble bust of an ancient ancestor. The stone head disintegrated in a spray of white powder and fragments, the force of the spell sending a shockwave through the room that rattled the windows in their frames.

"Thirty years!" She punched the wall beside her, her knuckles splitting open, crimson blood smearing across the polished stone. "Thirty years of playing god, of stitching this world together with lies and blood, just to watch it all unravel because of one fucking anomaly!

She began to pace like a caged predator, her movements erratic and violent. Every time her mind spiraled back to Rex Rexilion and the terrifying implications of that gap in his thread, she lashed out again.

She kicked a chair, sending it spinning across the room where it shattered against the wall. She swept her arm across a side table, sending silver goblets and enchanted artifacts crashing to the floor in a discordant symphony of breaking metal and glass.
Her breathing was ragged now, a series of harsh, desperate gasps. Sweat beaded on her forehead despite the chill of the room.
The sanctum, once a temple of order and absolute control, now looked like a battlefield. Smoke curled from the scorched patches on the floor where her magic had burned through the expensive rugs.
"Gods damn it all to hell," she whispered, the fury momentarily giving way to a hollow, aching exhaustion.
She slumped against a wall that was still smoking from her last outburst, her hands shaking uncontrollably. Blood dripped from her split knuckles, pooling on the floor.
She closed her eyes, but she couldn’t find darkness. All she saw was the void where Rex’s history should have been.
All she heard was Kaeleth’s warning, echoing in the ruins of her room like a curse.
"I will not fail," she hissed through clenched teeth, the words more a threat to herself than anyone else. "I will not let it end like this."
But as she stood there amidst the wreckage of her own making, surrounded by the broken bones of her sanctuary, the truth remained: she had never been more terrified in her entire life.

The destruction inside the sanctum was no longer a release; it had become a ritual of pure, unadulterated madness. Celestina wasn’t just breaking objects anymore; she was trying to break reality itself.
"WHY NOW?" she screamed, her voice reaching a register that sounded less human and more like a banshee’s wail. "WHY DOES THE UNIVERSE DECIDE TO BEND JUST WHEN I HAVE IT ALL UNDER CONTROL?"

A massive shockwave of violet energy exploded from her core, sending a ripple through the floorboards that made the entire wing of the palace shudder. The stone floor beneath her feet spiderwebbed with cracks as she slammed both palms downward.
"I WILL NOT BE DEFEATED BY A SHADOW! AND I WILL NOT BE HUMILIATED BY A GHOST IN THE TIMELINE!"
The air in the room began to ionize, smelling of burnt metal and ozone. Sparks of raw energy danced across her skin like angry insects.

She grabbed a heavy silver candelabra and hurled it at the wall with such supernatural force that it didn’t just dent the stone; it embedded itself six inches deep into the masonry before exploding into molten droplets.

"FUCK THE UNCERTAINTY! FUCK THE RISK! FUCK KAELETH AND HIS GODDAMN WARNINGS!" she shrieked, her eyes glowing with an unstable, terrifying light. "IF THE WORLD WANTS TO BURN, THEN I WILL BE THE ONE TO LIGHT THE MATCH!"

She spun in a circle, her energy flaring outward in a continuous, rotating vortex of destruction. Bookshelves were ripped from their moorings and shredded; tapestries were incinerated mid-air; the very air seemed to scream as her magic tore through it.

Meanwhile, three corridors away, two Legionnaires Kael and Jace were trudging down the hallway toward the armory. Kael was complaining about his boots, while Jace was halfway through a story about a tavern maid.
"I’m telling you, Jace, the girl had eyes like—" Kael stopped mid-sentence.
A low, subsonic rumble rolled through the floorboards. It wasn’t the kind of rumble that came from an earthquake; it was the kind of rumble that came from something fundamental being violated.
Then came the sound: a wet, bone-crushing CRUNCH followed immediately by a scream that sounded like it had been dragged through gravel.
"Was that... Lady Celestina’s wing?" Jace asked, his face draining of color.
"Shh," Kael hissed, holding up a hand. "Maybe it’s just training exercises.
BOOM.
A thunderclap erupted from somewhere ahead. The chandelier hanging from the ceiling twenty feet away rattled violently, its crystals chiming in panic.
A gout of violet flame licked out from under the massive obsidian doors of Celestina’s sanctum, seeping through the cracks like poisonous blood.
The two soldiers froze. The hallway suddenly felt very cold.
"That’s not training," Jace whispered, his voice cracking. "That sounds like she’s trying to murder the building."
Another crash followed the unmistakable sound of something heavy, like a marble statue, being pulverized into dust. Then came the voice.
It wasn’t the composed, terrifyingly calm Celestina they knew. It was a voice of pure, unhinged catastrophe.
"I’LL TEAR THE STARS FROM THE SKY BEFORE I LET THIS FAIL!" the voice roared from behind the doors. "EVERYTHING IS A LIE! EVERYTHING IS A FUCKING TRAP!"
Kael and Jace shared a look of pure, unadulterated terror. Kael slowly raised a hand and pointed toward the opposite exit.
"Jace," Kael said quietly.
"Yeah?"
"On three."
"One."
"Two."
"THREE!"

The two Legionnaires turned on their heels with such synchronized desperation that they nearly tripped over each other. They didn’t run; they scrambled, their armor clanking frantically as they bolted in the opposite direction, boots skidding on the marble.
"I DIDN’T SEE ANYTHING!" Jace yelled as they sprinted down the corridor. "I WAS NEVER IN THIS WING! I DON’T EVEN KNOW WHAT SHE IS!"
"KEEP RUNNING!" Kael bellowed back, his lungs burning. "IF SHE COMES OUT OF THAT ROOM, WE’RE DEAD BEFORE WE CAN EVEN PRAY TO THE GODS!"
Behind them, another explosion rocked the palace, followed by the sound of Celestina screaming something about the fundamental inadequacy of the mortal plane. The two men didn’t look back.
They ran as if the hounds of hell themselves were at their heels, because in that moment, they knew: whatever was happening behind those obsidian doors was far worse.

chapters.title: Chapter 893. Seems Like I Have To Show My Martial Arts By Kicking Her Soldiers’ Asses!
paragraphs: The training hall was a cathedral of disciplined violence. Its floors consisted of reinforced hardwood planks laid over ancient stone, a specialized construction designed to absorb the bone-jarring impact of a fall while maintaining the unforgiving consistency required for elite footwork.

As Rex stepped onto the surface, his mind immediately processed the data. The Martial Arts Mastery system flickered across his vision in ghostly amber text, automatically cataloging the floor’s coefficient of friction, its elasticity, and its structural integrity.
The system began the silent process of calibrating his subconscious stance, adjusting the micro movements of his ankles and knees to match the specific give of the wood.
Twelve fighters stood in a loose, predatory formation. These were not mere soldiers; they were Aurelia’s elite, the scalpel she used when the hammer proved too blunt.

They had been mid-session when Rex arrived, their bodies already slick with sweat, their breathing synchronized. Their eyes fell on him not with hostility, but with the cold, clinical assessment of wolves sizing up a new predator that had wandered into their territory.
It was a professional scrutiny, weighing his center of gravity, his shoulder tension, and the way his weight distributed across his soles.
To the side, Aurelia stood with a composed authority. Behind her, Diana, Iris, and Elaris formed a silent phalanx of observers.
Aurelia didn’t look like a commander preparing for war; she looked like an architect watching a test subject enter a stress chamber.
Rex took his position in the dead center of the hall. The silence was absolute, broken only by the faint creak of wood beneath his boots.
He looked at the twelve, meeting each of their stares with a calm that bordered on the unsettling.
"Full contact," Aurelia’s voice cut through the stillness like a blade. "Standard martial disciplines only."
"No working magic... No system abilities... and no magical enhancement." Aurelia raised his fist. "I want it to be only purely physical brute force that only relies on your martial arts!"
Rex met her gaze. "Agreed."

"One more condition," Aurelia added, her eyes narrowing slightly. "If you break them or if you incapacitate them to the point where they cannot walk out of this hall under their own power, I will consider that a failure of your judgment rather than a testament to your capability."
"I want to see your skill, Rex..."
"I do not want to spend my afternoon cleaning blood off the floorboards and filling out infirmary reports."
Rex considered the request. His inner monologue ran through the tactical implications: ’Twelve opponents. High-tier conditioning. Limited to raw physicality.’
’The margin for error is razor thin...’
’One miscalculated strike could shatter a clavicle or rupture an organ.’
"That is a reasonable condition," Rex said aloud, his voice steady and devoid of arrogance. "I have no interest in maiming people who are simply performing their duties."
"Good," Aurelia said, stepping back to give them space. "Then begin whenever you are ready."
"My unit does not wait for a formal signal because they move when they see an opening."
Rex braced himself. His muscles coiled.
The system’s calibration finished, locking his body into a state of perfect readiness. The twelve fighters shifted simultaneously in a single, fluid movement of leather and sinew.
The air in the room suddenly felt heavier, charged with the kinetic potential of twelve bodies about to explode into motion. The assessment was over.
The hunt had begun.
Aurelia watched Rex settle into his stance, and for a moment, the composed commander flickered. A dark, almost imperceptible hunger stirred beneath her professional exterior.
Her initial condition, the warning about restraint, felt suddenly hollow, like a leash she had placed on a predator she secretly wanted to see unleashed.
’No,’ she thought, her fingers curling slightly at her sides. ’Not restraint... Not today...’
She had seen the footage of Rex’s confrontation with the dragon. She had seen how he moved, not like a man fighting for survival, but like a force of nature correcting an error in reality.

She had seen the way bones had shattered under his grip and how blood had sprayed like crimson rain. The memory of that raw, unfiltered violence burned in her mind, and she found herself craving to see it directed at her own elite.
She wanted to see if her best could withstand the sheer, crushing inevitability of his strength.
Leaning slightly toward Elaris, who stood just behind her, Aurelia spoke in a voice so low it barely carried past their immediate circle. "Mother."
Elaris shifted her attention instantly, her eyes bright with alertness. "Yes, my dear Aurelia?"
"Stand closer to the perimeter," Aurelia commanded, her words hushed but carrying an edge of something dangerous. "Prepare a high-grade cellular regeneration spell."
"I want you primed for immediate intervention, but do not interfere unless I give the word..."
"We may need to patch up some... structural damage."

Elaris blinked, her gaze flickering toward Rex, then back to Aurelia. She caught the subtle shift in the commander’s demeanor, the way her pupils had dilated slightly, the way her breathing had deepened.
The implications were clear: the gloves were coming off.
"You want me to prepare for serious injury?" Elaris whispered, her voice tinged with apprehension. "But you said--"
"I changed my mind," Aurelia interrupted, her eyes never leaving Rex. "I want to see the true extent of his lethality."
"I want to see what happens when he stops holding back."
"Don’t let me stop you from healing them, Mother... Just make sure they don’t die."
Elaris swallowed hard, her hands already beginning to glow with a faint, warm amber light as she prepared her mana. "Understood."
The shift in atmosphere was instantaneous. The twelve fighters, trained to read their commander’s every microexpression, felt the change like a sudden drop in barometric pressure.
Among them, the reactions split down the middle.
Bobby, a scarred veteran with a reputation for being unbreakable, felt a surge of adrenaline that made his blood sing. A feral grin touched his lips.
He had heard the stories of Rex’s brutality; he wanted to feel that power against his own ribs. He wanted to see if he could survive the impact of a man who fought dragons.
To him, this wasn’t just training; it was a test of his very existence.

But beside him, two younger recruits visibly paled. Their eyes darted to Rex’s hands, hands that had torn through scales thicker than steel, and then to his stance, which seemed to absorb the very light around him.

They remembered the reports from the island assessment as well: the sound of bones snapping like dry kindling, the wet crunch of cartilage being pulverized. Their hearts hammered against their ribs, not with excitement, but with the primal terror of prey realizing the trap has been sprung.

Rex, oblivious to the internal schism of his opponents but hyperaware of the shift in their biometrics through the system, narrowed his eyes. He could see their heart rates spiking and could see the micro tremors in the legs of the nervous recruits.
The tension in the room had gone from controlled to volatile.
The air felt thick, charged with the unspoken permission for violence.
Aurelia’s lips curled into the faintest, most dangerous smile. She had given them the illusion of safety, but she had just privately revoked it.
She wanted to see the carnage. She wanted to see Rex Rexilion break them.
"Begin," Aurelia said, though her voice lacked its earlier caution. It sounded less like a command and more like an invitation to a massacre.
The silence that followed Aurelia’s command was not empty; it was a pressurized chamber, a vacuum waiting to be filled by the first scream.
The twelve elite fighters didn’t move as individuals. They moved as a single organism, a collective consciousness forged through years of shared blood and synchronized training.
Without a word spoken, without so much as a glance exchanged, they communicated through microgestures: the subtle tilt of a chin, the minute shift of a shoulder blade.
They were reading the new reality: the Commander’s unspoken permission for violence had changed the stakes from a test of skill to a test of survival.

The woman at the left edge of the formation, Karys, acted as the unit’s neural center. Her posture was flawless, her stillness absolute; she was the standard against which every other member of the Legion measured their own competence.
With a sharp, almost imperceptible flick of her wrist, she signaled the initiation of their combat geometry.
Then, they spread.

It wasn’t the chaotic rush of a mob or the desperate scramble of frightened men. It was a calculated, mathematical expansion. They flowed outward like spilled mercury, each fighter finding their precise coordinates on the hardwood floor.
The movement was beautiful in its lethal efficiency, each step measured to maintain optimal distance while closing the net around their target.
Rex didn’t blink. His pupils dilated as his martial arts mastery went into overdrive, the system’s amber text flooding his peripheral vision with raw tactical data.
The passive efficiency of the skill allowed him to process their positioning not as twelve separate threats, but as a single, interlocking machine.
’Three seconds,’ his mind noted with cold detachment. ’Pattern identified...’
The architecture of their attack crystallized in his mind: a three-tiered wave system designed to overwhelm and encircle.
