"I want it to be only purely physical brute force that only relies on your martial arts!"
Rex met her gaze.
"Agreed."
"One more condition," Aurelia added, her eyes narrowing slightly.

"If you break them or if you incapacitate them to the point where they cannot walk out of this hall under their own power, I will consider that a failure of your judgment rather than a testament to your capability."
"I want to see your skill, Rex..."
"I do not want to spend my afternoon cleaning blood off the floorboards and filling out infirmary reports."
Rex considered the request.
His inner monologue ran through the tactical implications: ’Twelve opponents.
High-tier conditioning.
Limited to raw physicality.’
’The margin for error is razor thin...’
’One miscalculated strike could shatter a clavicle or rupture an organ.’
"That is a reasonable condition," Rex said aloud, his voice steady and devoid of arrogance.
"I have no interest in maiming people who are simply performing their duties."
"Good," Aurelia said, stepping back to give them space.
"Then begin whenever you are ready."
"My unit does not wait for a formal signal because they move when they see an opening."
Rex braced himself.
His muscles coiled.
The system’s calibration finished, locking his body into a state of perfect readiness.
The twelve fighters shifted simultaneously in a single, fluid movement of leather and sinew.
The air in the room suddenly felt heavier, charged with the kinetic potential of twelve bodies about to explode into motion.
The assessment was over.
The hunt had begun.
Aurelia watched Rex settle into his stance, and for a moment, the composed commander flickered.
A dark, almost imperceptible hunger stirred beneath her professional exterior.
Her initial condition, the warning about restraint, felt suddenly hollow, like a leash she had placed on a predator she secretly wanted to see unleashed.
’No,’ she thought, her fingers curling slightly at her sides. ’Not restraint...
Not today...’
She had seen the footage of Rex’s confrontation with the dragon.
She had seen how he moved, not like a man fighting for survival, but like a force of nature correcting an error in reality.
She had seen the way bones had shattered under his grip and how blood had sprayed like crimson rain.
The memory of that raw, unfiltered violence burned in her mind, and she found herself craving to see it directed at her own elite.
She wanted to see if her best could withstand the sheer, crushing inevitability of his strength.
Leaning slightly toward Elaris, who stood just behind her, Aurelia spoke in a voice so low it barely carried past their immediate circle.
"Mother."
Elaris shifted her attention instantly, her eyes bright with alertness.
"Yes, my dear Aurelia?"
"Stand closer to the perimeter," Aurelia commanded, her words hushed but carrying an edge of something dangerous.
"Prepare a high-grade cellular regeneration spell."
"I want you primed for immediate intervention, but do not interfere unless I give the word..."
"We may need to patch up some... structural damage."
Elaris blinked, her gaze flickering toward Rex, then back to Aurelia.
She caught the subtle shift in the commander’s demeanor, the way her pupils had dilated slightly, the way her breathing had deepened.
The implications were clear: the gloves were coming off.
"You want me to prepare for serious injury?" Elaris whispered, her voice tinged with apprehension.
"But you said--"
"I changed my mind," Aurelia interrupted, her eyes never leaving Rex.
"I want to see the true extent of his lethality."
"I want to see what happens when he stops holding back."
"Don’t let me stop you from healing them, Mother...
Just make sure they don’t die."
Elaris swallowed hard, her hands already beginning to glow with a faint, warm amber light as she prepared her mana.
"Understood."
The shift in atmosphere was instantaneous.
The twelve fighters, trained to read their commander’s every microexpression, felt the change like a sudden drop in barometric pressure.
Among them, the reactions split down the middle.
Bobby, a scarred veteran with a reputation for being unbreakable, felt a surge of adrenaline that made his blood sing.
A feral grin touched his lips.
He had heard the stories of Rex’s brutality; he wanted to feel that power against his own ribs.
He wanted to see if he could survive the impact of a man who fought dragons.
To him, this wasn’t just training; it was a test of his very existence.
But beside him, two younger recruits visibly paled.
Their eyes darted to Rex’s hands, hands that had torn through scales thicker than steel, and then to his stance, which seemed to absorb the very light around him.
They remembered the reports from the island assessment as well: the sound of bones snapping like dry kindling, the wet crunch of cartilage being pulverized.
Their hearts hammered against their ribs, not with excitement, but with the primal terror of prey realizing the trap has been sprung.
Rex, oblivious to the internal schism of his opponents but hyperaware of the shift in their biometrics through the system, narrowed his eyes.
He could see their heart rates spiking and could see the micro tremors in the legs of the nervous recruits.
The tension in the room had gone from controlled to volatile.
The air felt thick, charged with the unspoken permission for violence.
Aurelia’s lips curled into the faintest, most dangerous smile.
She had given them the illusion of safety, but she had just privately revoked it.
She wanted to see the carnage.
She wanted to see Rex Rexilion break them.
"Begin," Aurelia said, though her voice lacked its earlier caution.
It sounded less like a command and more like an invitation to a massacre.
The silence that followed Aurelia’s command was not empty; it was a pressurized chamber, a vacuum waiting to be filled by the first scream.
The twelve elite fighters didn’t move as individuals.
They moved as a single organism, a collective consciousness forged through years of shared blood and synchronized training.
Without a word spoken, without so much as a glance exchanged, they communicated through microgestures: the subtle tilt of a chin, the minute shift of a shoulder blade.
They were reading the new reality: the Commander’s unspoken permission for violence had changed the stakes from a test of skill to a test of survival.
The woman at the left edge of the formation, Karys, acted as the unit’s neural center.
Her posture was flawless, her stillness absolute; she was the standard against which every other member of the Legion measured their own competence.
With a sharp, almost imperceptible flick of her wrist, she signaled the initiation of their combat geometry.
Then, they spread.
It wasn’t the chaotic rush of a mob or the desperate scramble of frightened men.
It was a calculated, mathematical expansion.
They flowed outward like spilled mercury, each fighter finding their precise coordinates on the hardwood floor.
The movement was beautiful in its lethal efficiency, each step measured to maintain optimal distance while closing the net around their target.
Rex didn’t blink.
His pupils dilated as his martial arts mastery went into overdrive, the system’s amber text flooding his peripheral vision with raw tactical data.
The passive efficiency of the skill allowed him to process their positioning not as twelve separate threats, but as a single, interlocking machine.
’Three seconds,’ his mind noted with cold detachment. ’Pattern identified...’
The architecture of their attack crystallized in his mind: a three-tiered wave system designed to overwhelm and encircle.

chapters.title: Chapter 894. Just Gotta Fight Serious For A Bit... Nothing To Gory... Maybe.
paragraphs: The first four of the Vanguard were already breaking into a sprint, their boots thundering against the hardwood. They were the hammer, designed to engage Rex directly, forcing him into a defensive posture and creating chaos through sheer physical pressure.

The next four in the support layer were moving into flanking positions, angling themselves to exploit any opening the Vanguard created. Their role was to intercept Rex if he attempted to slip past the first wave, cutting off escape routes and applying pressure from the angles.

In the final four, the Reserves remained slightly behind the others, moving with a controlled urgency. They were the safety net, the tactical response force ready to plug any gaps or reinforce a failing position.
’Four... four... four...’ Rex analyzed, his breathing slowing even as his adrenaline spiked. ’A textbook encirclement pattern optimized for single target neutralization.’
’They expect me to defend, to retreat, to get trapped...’
’They are fighting a human opponent and they have not yet realized they are fighting a catastrophe.
His inner monologue remained eerily calm, a stark contrast to the storm brewing in the room. ’The Vanguard will come fast, high-impact, low-finesse...’
’The Support will try to hamstring my mobility...’
’The Reserves will wait for the moment of exhaustion...’
’I need to shatter the first wave quickly to disrupt the entire geometry...’
’If the first four fall, the architecture collapses.’
Aurelia leaned forward, her breath catching in her throat. She could see it the way Rex wasn’t bracing for a fight but simply occupying the space where the fight would happen.
He looked less like a combatant and more like a fixed point around which the world was about to break.

The first wave was thirty feet away. Their faces were masks of grim determination, some hungry for the glory of the struggle, others hollowed out by the dawning realization of what was about to unfold.
The air screamed as they closed the distance.

Rex planted his feet, his weight settling into the floor as the system calibrated his center of gravity for the inevitable impact. He waited for the first blow, the first crack of bone, the first taste of the violence he had been invited to unleash.
The first wave struck like a coordinated detonation.

Marren was the first to breach Rex’s perimeter. He moved with the terrifying, controlled explosiveness of a predator, all kinetic energy channeled through a perfectly synchronized chain of muscle and bone.
His strike was clean, a textbook entry designed to overwhelm a target with pure momentum.
Rex didn’t retreat. He didn’t brace for impact.
His Martial Arts Mastery flashed a critical data point in his peripheral vision: Leverage Point: Right Brachial Axis. Redirection Efficiency: 98%.

Rex stepped inside the arc of Marren’s strike, his movement so precise it seemed almost ghostly. He didn’t block; he simply placed a single hand at the exact pivot point where Marren’s momentum was most vulnerable.
With a subtle, violent twist of his wrist and shoulder, Rex redirected the force.
Marren didn’t just miss; he was violently slung sideways. His own momentum became his enemy, hurling him across the hardwood as if he had been struck by a runaway carriage.
He crashed into the floor with a bone-jarring thud, skidding several feet before his training instincts kicked in, allowing him to roll and absorb the impact rather than breaking his neck.
"First point," Aurelia’s voice rang out, cold and clinical as she scored the exchange from the sidelines. "Marren, your entry was flawless, but your recovery was sluggish."
"You left your flank exposed for three tenths of a second too long."
Marren gasped for air as he pushed himself up, his ribs aching from the sudden deceleration. He said nothing. In this arena, words were wasted energy; only survival mattered.

The second and third fighters Mael and Sela erupted from opposite angles simultaneously. This was the Support Layer’s immediate response: if the first man failed, the next two would overwhelm the target before he could reset.
To any other fighter, this would require a parallel defense, splitting attention between two threats. But Rex’s processing speed allowed him to treat them as a sequence.
Mael came in with a straight, direct thrust, a committed strike meant to punch through Rex’s guard. Rex didn’t telegraph his movement.

He waited until Mael was within the ’Red Zone,’ the range where the cost of redirection was minimal, and then he pivoted. With the economy of a predator, Rex caught Mael’s wrist and shoulder, turning his forward momentum ninety degrees.
Mael flew past Rex like wind caught in a sail, stumbling past without touching a single inch of Rex’s body.
Half a second later, Sela arrived. She was faster than Mael, her mind already processing the failure of her comrade.

She saw Rex’s position shifting and immediately adjusted her trajectory mid-sprint, angling her strike to intercept where Rex would be. It was a brilliant tactical adjustment, one that would have caught any ordinary master.
But Sela was calculating based on a human’s reaction time. Rex was operating beyond it.
Her strike carved through empty air. Rex had already vacated the space she was targeting, his body having already begun its rotation toward her before she even finished her adjustment.
The gap between her assumption and his reality was a chasm.
Rex didn’t wait for her to recover. He punished her instinct before she could capitalize on it.
As she stumbled forward from the missed strike, Rex’s palm connected with her solar plexus not with a punch but with a precise, explosive burst of force designed to collapse the diaphragm.

Sela hit the floor hard, the air leaving her lungs in a pained wheeze. Even as she collapsed, her eyes remained locked on Rex, her mind already racing to formulate a counterstrategy even as her body screamed in protest.
"Sela," Aurelia called out, her voice carrying a rare note of grudging approval. "That recovery instinct is the only reason you aren’t still unconscious on the floor."
"Your adjustment was perfect, but your timing was human... Against him, ’human’ is a death sentence."
Rex stood motionless in the center of the hall, his breathing as steady as if he were standing in a garden. His inner monologue remained cold and analytical. ’Three down... Nine to go.’
’The Vanguard is depleted, but the Support Layer is already recalibrating.’
’They aren’t panicked; they’re learning...’
’That makes them more dangerous...’
’They’re beginning to realize that they can’t fight him; they can only hope to survive him.’

The other nine fighters began to close in, their movements no longer just coordinated but desperate. The air in the room grew thick with the metallic tang of sweat and the unspoken promise of breaking bones.

The fourth fighter came low, moving like a shadow across the hardwood. Rex recognized the signature of his approach immediately through the system’s analysis: this wasn’t brute force; this was technical predation.

The man was the unit’s specialist in close-quarters grappling and ground-level takedowns. His technique was a sophisticated trap, a lightning-fast ankle sweep designed to sever Rex’s foundation, immediately followed by a body grab to pin him while he was off balance.
It was a move designed to exploit the momentary weight shift a fighter makes after engaging three consecutive opponents.
But Rex didn’t play by the rules of human momentum.

In the quarter second before contact, his Martial Arts Mastery triggered a micro adjustment. His weight didn’t just shift; it redistributed with impossible fluidity, rising slightly onto the balls of his feet.
The sweep struck air. The specialist’s leg passed harmlessly beneath Rex’s lifted calf.

Desperate to complete the sequence, the fighter lunged upward to execute the body grab. His hands tore at Rex’s clothes, but instead of finding the soft give of the torso, they collided with the iron-hard cordage of Rex’s forearm.
The leverage differential was catastrophic. The grab was calibrated to crush ribs and control a center of mass; against a forearm, it was useless, leaving the specialist exposed and overextended.
In one smooth motion, Rex’s hand shot down like a piston. He didn’t punch; he seized the fighter’s wrist and collar in a vice grip.
The specialist’s eyes widened as he realized he was no longer the hunter but a puppet caught in a snare.
Rex didn’t throw him. A throw would have sent him crashing into the stone walls with a bone-splintering impact.

Instead, Rex performed a controlled deposition; he simply placed the man back on the floor with the terrifying precision of someone who had decided that the lesson was not in the pain of the impact but in the absolute helplessness of the failed technique.
"That was generous," Aurelia’s voice cut through the sudden silence, colder than before. "Do not mistake restraint for weakness."
"Do not get used to generosity because the world outside this hall will not set you down gently; it will grind you into the dirt."
The specialist stayed on one knee, breathing hard, staring at his own shaking hands. He had been neutralized without Rex even breaking a sweat.
Then, the second wave arrived.
These four moved differently. The raw, reckless confidence of the Vanguard had evaporated, replaced by something far more dangerous: professional caution.
They moved in a staggered formation, each keeping a watchful eye on their companions while maintaining a measured distance. They were assessing, probing, waiting for the moment Rex overextended.
Rex watched them through the amber HUD of his mind.
’Caution,’ he thought bitterly. ’A double-edged blade...’
’You’ve learned not to rush into his reach, but in doing so, you’ve lost the one thing that could hurt him: commitment.’
’You’re hesitating. And in a fight against someone who moves faster than thought, hesitation is where you die.’

chapters.title: Chapter 895. They’re Starting To Show Some Efforts... But It’s Still Not Enough!
paragraphs: The Support Layer was trying to play a game of chess, but Rex was playing a game of slaughter. They were trying to minimize risk, but they were also minimizing the very force required to actually penetrate his defense.
They were pulling their punches before they had even thrown them.
Rex didn’t wait for them to find their courage. He didn’t wait for them to test his guard.

With a predator’s smile that never reached his eyes, Rex began to advance. He didn’t circle; he walked directly into the heart of their caution, forcing them to react to his approach, forcing them to break their careful distance, and forcing them to choose between maintaining their formation or defending themselves.
He walked straight into the trap they were trying to set, knowing full well he was the one who would spring it.
Rex didn’t wait for them to close the distance; he invaded it.
By advancing aggressively, he shattered the very foundation of their caution. Caution requires control over distance, control over timing, and control over the engagement’s tempo.

By walking directly into their space, Rex stripped them of those luxuries, forcing them to react to him on his terms rather than theirs. He turned their measured approach into a panicked scramble for survival.
The second wave adapted. They were elite for a reason; they didn’t freeze.
Instead, they tightened their formation, their movements becoming more economical, more coiled.
But they were trying to adapt to a human. Rex was adapting to a mathematical certainty.

His martial arts mastery didn’t just predict their movements; it rendered them obsolete. The system didn’t see a sequence of punches or kicks; it saw a cascade of probability, a pattern that had already committed to its next three seconds of existence before the fighters themselves had even consciously decided on them.
Rex wasn’t reacting to what they were doing; he was occupying the space where they would be doing it.

The first fighter of this wave launched a calibrated four-strike combination: three rapid jabs building momentum toward a devastating fourth blow designed to land while Rex was still reeling from the initial assault.
Rex saw the fourth strike before the first had even left the fighter’s shoulder.

Instead of blocking, which would have required absorbing the energy, Rex moved to interrupt the rhythm. He stepped into the microscopic gap between the second and third strikes, a moment of perfect vulnerability where the fighter’s weight was suspended between movements.
The interruption was brutal. Rex’s shoulder collided with the fighter’s sternum with the force of a battering ram.

The fighter’s ribs gave way with a wet, sickening crack, the sound echoing through the hall like breaking timber. The man’s own momentum betrayed him, sending him stumbling through his own unfinished combination, his lungs seizing as Rex guided the broken stumble all the way to the floor.
Immediately, the second and third fighters synchronized. This was the pincer, a coordinated high-low attack designed to overwhelm Rex’s guard by attacking two different planes simultaneously.

Rex read both trajectories in the same millisecond. He chose to address the low attack first not because it carried more threat, but because the mechanics of the countermove placed his body in a position that made the high attack physically impossible to land.
As he swept the low fighter’s leg, his body rotated with such violent precision that the high fighter’s strike found nothing but empty air where Rex’s skull had been moments before.
The two fighters hit the floor in rapid succession, one crashing down from a leg sweep, the other tumbling from the loss of balance.
"Two more down," Aurelia whispered, her eyes tracking the crimson spray that had just painted a section of the hardwood. "But they’re learning...
"They’re starting to see the gaps."
The third wave, the Reserves remained motionless. They were the most dangerous predators in the room because they were the most patient.

They watched with cold, analytical detachment, their minds cataloging every microexpression, every shift in Rex’s stance. They were waiting for the data, gathering the intelligence that would allow them to execute the perfect response to whatever the first eight had failed to accomplish.
Rex turned his attention back to the remaining two fighters of the second wave.
He allowed them to see what they wanted to see. He let them believe they had found the flaw in his defense, the perfect angle to exploit.
He deliberately shifted his stance, exposing a sliver of his flank, making the opening look tantalizingly vulnerable.
’Go ahead,’ Rex thought, his inner voice as cold as a winter grave. ’Take the bait...’
’Walk into the slaughter.

He had read that ’opening’ six seconds before they had even noticed it. He had been maneuvering toward that exact moment, sculpting the battlefield to ensure that when they exploited the angle, they would be walking directly into a meat grinder.
They saw the opening. They saw their chance to salvage the unit’s honor.
And with desperate, hungry eyes, they exploited it.

At full potential, Rex’s Martial Arts Mastery ceased to be a library of techniques and became something far more terrifying: it became a living equation of violence. It wasn’t just knowing how to punch; it was knowing the exact molecular consequence of every possible movement.
When the two remaining fighters of the second wave lunged into the trap he had meticulously laid, they weren’t just attacking; they were delivering themselves into a meat grinder.

The response to a coordinated two-person exploitation, when the target has already anticipated the trap, is a single, devastatingly precise maneuver: using the first attacker’s committed momentum to become a physical barrier against the second.
Rex spun, his body a blur of controlled violence. He caught the first fighter’s wrist while simultaneously driving his elbow into the second’s ribs.

The first fighter’s momentum was redirected into his partner’s chest with the force of a sledgehammer. There was a wet, crunching sound as ribs splintered like dry kindling, followed by the sickening gurgle of punctured lungs.
Both fighters collapsed, their bodies convulsing as they hit the floor in a tangle of broken limbs and labored breaths.
Eight fighters down. The hardwood was no longer pristine; it was slick with sweat and splatters of crimson.

Diana, watching from the periphery, had fallen into a deathly silence. She wasn’t just observing a sparring match anymore; she was witnessing something primal, something that defied her understanding of the man she loved.
Her pupils were dilated, her breath shallow, as she watched Rex move through the carnage with the cold, mechanical precision of an executioner. She was recalibrating her entire reality.
Then, the third wave arrived.
Rex looked up at them over the broken forms of the eight who lay scattered across the floor, some gasping for air, others clutching shattered bones. His gaze was flat, devoid of malice or triumph.
He looked at the final four with the detached curiosity of a scientist observing a new strain of virus. He was genuinely interested to see if they had learned anything from the blood spilled.
They didn’t come in a spread. They came in a phalanx.

This was not the unit’s standard tactical approach. These four moved in a tight, overlapping formation, shoulders nearly touching, moving as a single, multi-limbed organism rather than four individuals.
Rex’s assessment flashed across his mind: ’The smartest four...’
’They saw that individual approach equals failure...’
’They have chosen mass over maneuverability.’

A tight formation solved the problem of individual exploitation, but it birthed a new vulnerability: catastrophic commitment. Their combined momentum was immense, but their ability to adapt to sudden changes in direction was severely compromised by the need to maintain their structural cohesion.
They were a juggernaut, powerful but linear.
"Good," Aurelia whispered, her voice barely audible over the ragged breathing of the fallen. "That is the right idea."
"Let us see if the idea has teeth."
Rex waited. He waited until they were two steps from contact, until the air between them hummed with the displaced pressure of their approach.
Then, he stepped aside.
It was a single, economical movement, the bare minimum displacement required to vacate the kill zone. The formation’s combined momentum carried all four past him like a tidal wave passing a boulder.
They were skilled enough to avoid crashing into each other, but their trajectory was now committed. They had sailed past their target.
For four seconds, they were caught in the deadly limbo of reorientation—the time it takes a formation to pivot, reverse, and reengage.
To a normal human, four seconds is a lifetime of hesitation. To Rex, four seconds was an eternity of opportunity.
He struck before they had even completed half their arc.
His first target was the lead fighter of the formation. Rex’s strike wasn’t aimed at the face or chest; it was a surgical strike to the shoulder joint.

With a sharp, cracking pop, the joint dislocated, the tendons tearing like old rope. The fighter’s arm went limp, instantly destroying the structural stability needed to maintain the formation’s momentum.
The phalanx began to fray at the point of contact, the integrity of the unit unraveling like a rope with its primary strand severed.
The second fighter reacted instinctively, attempting to close the gap left by her collapsing comrade. It was a correct tactical instinct, but it was executed half a second too late.

They were trying to minimize risk, but they were also minimizing the very force required to actually penetrate his defense.
They were pulling their punches before they had even thrown them.
Rex didn’t wait for them to find their courage.
He didn’t wait for them to test his guard.
With a predator’s smile that never reached his eyes, Rex began to advance.

He didn’t circle; he walked directly into the heart of their caution, forcing them to react to his approach, forcing them to break their careful distance, and forcing them to choose between maintaining their formation or defending themselves.
He walked straight into the trap they were trying to set, knowing full well he was the one who would spring it.
Rex didn’t wait for them to close the distance; he invaded it.
By advancing aggressively, he shattered the very foundation of their caution.
Caution requires control over distance, control over timing, and control over the engagement’s tempo.
By walking directly into their space, Rex stripped them of those luxuries, forcing them to react to him on his terms rather than theirs.
He turned their measured approach into a panicked scramble for survival.
The second wave adapted.
They were elite for a reason; they didn’t freeze.
Instead, they tightened their formation, their movements becoming more economical, more coiled.
But they were trying to adapt to a human.
Rex was adapting to a mathematical certainty.
His martial arts mastery didn’t just predict their movements; it rendered them obsolete.

The system didn’t see a sequence of punches or kicks; it saw a cascade of probability, a pattern that had already committed to its next three seconds of existence before the fighters themselves had even consciously decided on them.
Rex wasn’t reacting to what they were doing; he was occupying the space where they would be doing it.

The first fighter of this wave launched a calibrated four-strike combination: three rapid jabs building momentum toward a devastating fourth blow designed to land while Rex was still reeling from the initial assault.
Rex saw the fourth strike before the first had even left the fighter’s shoulder.

He stepped into the microscopic gap between the second and third strikes, a moment of perfect vulnerability where the fighter’s weight was suspended between movements.
The interruption was brutal.
Rex’s shoulder collided with the fighter’s sternum with the force of a battering ram.
The fighter’s ribs gave way with a wet, sickening crack, the sound echoing through the hall like breaking timber.

Immediately, the second and third fighters synchronized.
This was the pincer, a coordinated high-low attack designed to overwhelm Rex’s guard by attacking two different planes simultaneously.
Rex read both trajectories in the same millisecond.

He chose to address the low attack first not because it carried more threat, but because the mechanics of the countermove placed his body in a position that made the high attack physically impossible to land.
As he swept the low fighter’s leg, his body rotated with such violent precision that the high fighter’s strike found nothing but empty air where Rex’s skull had been moments before.

"They’re starting to see the gaps."

They were the most dangerous predators in the room because they were the most patient.

He allowed them to see what they wanted to see.
He let them believe they had found the flaw in his defense, the perfect angle to exploit.

’Walk into the slaughter.
He had read that ’opening’ six seconds before they had even noticed it.

chapters.title: Chapter 896. Six Seconds Is Longer Than Anyone Got, Still Not Enough
paragraphs: Rex was already occupying the space she was trying to fill, his body moving through the opening she had created. He met her mid-adjustment with a brutal palm strike to the sternum that sent her staggering backward, blood speckling her lips as her breath failed her.

The third fighter, desperate to salvage the unit’s cohesion, made the fatal mistake of committing to a full-force strike rather than focusing on reorientation. She threw everything she had into a desperate haymaker.

Rex met that commitment with the ultimate cunning of a predator who knows everything. He didn’t block; blocking would have wasted energy. Instead, he caught the arm and redirected the strike’s own terrifying force back into the fighter’s own body.
The momentum of her own attack tore through her shoulder socket, sending her spinning violently toward the floor in a spray of sweat and blood.
In less than two seconds, Rex had neutralized three of them before they could even finish turning around.

The fourth fighter, the final remaining threat, did not panic. As her three companions collapsed into the growing pool of crimson and broken bone, she completed her reorientation in two seconds instead of four.
She was exceptional.
Rilena did not fall into the trap of desperation. Unlike the others who had committed to singular, explosive techniques that Rex could easily dismantle, she maintained a fluid, predatory circling.

She threw shallow, probing strikes, ghostly jabs that weren’t meant to connect but to test the tension in Rex’s muscles, to gauge the exact millisecond his reflexes triggered. When Rex responded with minimal movement, a deliberate, calculated economy of motion, she didn’t misinterpret it as an opening.
She read his restraint as data. She understood that a predator who doesn’t flinch is a predator who has already won.
"That is Rilena," Aurelia said, her voice carrying a rare note of genuine academic fascination. "She has been with the unit longer than anyone else standing."
"Watch her... Watch what she does when she stops probing."
Rilena struck. She exploded forward, changing levels twice in a single, seamless approach, a terrifying display of biomechanical control.

Most fighters would have lost their balance, their center of gravity shattered by the rapid shift from high- to low- to mid-level. To execute it cleanly required a level of trust in one’s own body that bordered on the supernatural.
She executed it with flawless precision.
Rex’s inner systems hummed with acknowledgment. His martial arts mastery flashed a warning: ’High tier threat detected...’
’Probability of successful engagement: 98%.’
For the first time in the session, Rex gave an opponent time. He allowed her six seconds of sustained engagement the longest any single fighter had lasted.
In those six seconds, the training hall became a blur of lethal motion. Rilena’s strikes were precise, aimed at nerve clusters and joints, forcing Rex to move with genuine purpose.

She landed two techniques: a vicious spinning heel kick that Rex had to catch mid-air and a lightning-fast elbow aimed at his temple that would have shattered the skull of any other man in the household.
But Rex was not any other man.

The resolution was not a grand explosion of violence, but something far more chilling: a quiet, surgical conclusion. After six seconds of confirming Rilena’s terrifying skill, Rex simply decided the test was over.
As she committed to a final, desperate strike, Rex didn’t block; he flowed. He caught her momentum, pivoted his hips with devastating torque, and redirected her entire kinetic force downward.

There was no bone breaking this time, only the wet thud of a body being placed precisely where it needed to be. Rilena hit the hardwood in a controlled roll, gasping for air, her eyes wide with the shock of having been read like an open book.

Rex stood alone in the center of the hall. Twelve fighters lay scattered around him like debris after a hurricane, some unconscious, some clutching broken ribs, some convulsing from the shock of impact.
His chest rose and fell in a measured, elevated rhythm, the specific breathing pattern of a man who had engaged in genuine combat, not the composed stillness of someone who had merely been playing.
Then, he raised his fist.

A sound tore from his throat, not a shout of anger, not a rehearsed victory cry, but something primal and involuntary. It was the raw, guttural roar of a predator who had asserted dominance over the pack.
The sound was visceral, echoing off the high ceilings and vibrating through the bones of everyone present.
The silence that followed was heavy enough to suffocate.
Diana made a sound from the sidelines, a small, broken whimper that she couldn’t suppress. She was caught between terror and an overwhelming, terrifying awe at the monster she loved.

Iris stood frozen, her mask of neutrality shattered; she was staring at Rex with a raw, exposed intensity that she could no longer hide. Elaris remained silent, her eyes darting between Rex and Aurelia, sensing the seismic shift in the room’s power dynamic.
Aurelia stood at the hall’s edge, arms crossed. Her expression wasn’t one of surprise but of profound recalibration.
She had expected to see talent; she had witnessed a force of nature.
"The dragon," Aurelia said finally.
Her voice was flat and direct, the tone she used when she was dismantling her own previous conclusions. "And Tremor... Yesterday..."
"I said those might have been situations where you were fortunate. That you had simply survived by chance."
Rex wiped a streak of someone else’s blood from his jaw, his eyes locking onto hers with terrifying clarity. "You said that."
Aurelia took a breath, the weight of her admission hanging in the blood-scented air.
"I was wrong," she said.

Rex met Aurelia’s gaze, and for a moment, the predator vanished. In its place was something almost human: a warm, faintly pleased expression, the kind one reserves for receiving a truth that costs the giver something precious.

"You were assessing with limited information," Rex said, his voice carrying through the blood-scented silence like a calm blade. "You were calculating variables while missing the fundamental constant."
"I was assessing with bias," Aurelia corrected immediately.
There was no defensiveness in her tone, only the clinical honesty of a scientist admitting a contaminated sample. "The bias produced an incomplete assessment."
"I saw a survivor where I should have seen a force."

Her eyes swept over the carnage; the twelve fighters were scattered across the hardwood like broken dolls. Some were still whimpering, fingers pressed against shattered ribs; others were staring at the ceiling with the glassy-eyed shock of those who had just touched death.
"Get up," Aurelia commanded.
Her voice wasn’t raised, but it carried the absolute authority of a queen addressing her subjects. "All of you!"
"Look at your wounds... Feel the failure in your bones." A pause. "You were outclassed."
"That is a fact... But what you do in the next sixty seconds determines whether you are victims of circumstance or students of war."
"Get the fuck up."

One by one, through gritted teeth and labored breaths, they began to rise. The sound of their movement, the shuffling of limbs, the wet slap of bloodied palms on wood, was the only soundtrack to their humiliation.
Aurelia turned her attention to the standard setter. "Rilena."
Rilena straightened, though her chest still heaved as she fought to reclaim her oxygen. "Yes, Mistress."
"Six seconds," Aurelia said, stepping closer to the woman who had pushed Rex further than anyone else that morning. "That is longer than anyone else received."
"What does that data point tell you?"
Rilena wiped a smear of blood from her split lip, her eyes bright with the adrenaline of a near miss. "That I was the closest to actually presenting a problem..."
"That I forced him to engage rather than simply react."
"Yes." Aurelia’s expression sharpened, cutting through any potential pride. "But it also tells you exactly how far you still have to go before six seconds becomes six minutes."
"Do not mistake a temporary reprieve for mastery..."
"I want you obsessing over that gap, the terrifying distance between where you are and where he is, not comforting yourself with the compliment hidden inside it."
The tension in the room shifted from the aftermath of violence to the weight of expectation.

Elaris stepped forward from the shadows of the observer’s position, her movements fluid and deliberate. She broke the circle of fallen warriors, walking toward the two powerhouses at the center of the hall.
"Aurelia," Elaris said, her voice cutting through the lingering hum of adrenaline.
Aurelia turned her head slightly, meeting Elaris’s steady stare. "I know what you’re thinking, Mother."
"You know what I am going to say," Elaris countered with a faint, knowing smile.
"Yes," Aurelia said, though she didn’t move to concede. "And I am not going to say it yet."

Elaris turned to Rex, speaking conversationally, as if they were discussing something as mundane as the weather rather than the fact that he had just systematically dismantled an elite unit. "She is going to say it eventually, Rex."
"She simply prefers to arrive at obvious conclusions through her own internal process rather than accepting them when they are handed to her on a silver platter."

Rex watched them, his breathing finally returning to a resting state, though his body still hummed with the residual electricity of the fight. He saw the unspoken words hanging between the two women: the acknowledgment of what he truly represented and what he truly was.
"I know," Rex said quietly.

chapters.title: Chapter 897. I Offered A Deal And Also A Dead Man’s Voice, Same Breath
paragraphs: Aurelia turned her piercing gaze toward Rex, her eyes reflecting the cold hunger of a strategist who had just seen a new weapon unveiled and immediately demanded to test its limits.
"I want to see more," she said, the words carrying the weight of an ultimatum. "I want to see what happens when the predator meets something that doesn’t break like glass."
Her eyes shifted, locking onto the figure standing in the shadows. "Iris."
Iris moved. She didn’t step so much as glide into the light, her movements carrying the practiced grace of someone who had spent years managing a volatile emotional landscape.
She had been watching Rex not as a student but as an observer gauging a potential catastrophe, and now she was being summoned to confront it.
"Sparring with Rex," Aurelia commanded, her voice echoing off the blood-stained walls. "Unarmed..."
"Show me the difference between raw power and disciplined restraint."
Iris didn’t respond immediately.
She simply looked at Rex. Her gaze was unreadable, a calm surface over a deep, churning ocean of grief and calculation.
Rex walked toward her. Each footfall on the blood-slicked hardwood sounded like a heartbeat in the sudden silence of the hall.
He stopped at the precise distance where their breathing would overlap close enough to feel the heat of another person, far enough to maintain the sanctity of a confrontation.
"I have a proposal," Rex said. His voice was low, intimate, and carried a dangerous undertone that made the air between them feel charged with static.
Iris tilted her head slightly, her eyes narrowing. She watched him with the flat, careful attention of a woman deciding whether to trust a lifeline or flinch from a blade.
"Speak."
"If you spar with me and lose," Rex said, his eyes locking onto hers with unshakable intensity, "you train with me... full integration and no reservations."
"You commit to the path you have already been considering in secret."
Iris didn’t flinch at the exposure, but her pupils dilated.
"And what is the alternative?" she asked, sensing the unspoken gravity behind his words. "Why would you offer terms instead of demands?"
"Because this isn’t just about combat anymore," Rex said.
He took half a step closer, lowering his voice so that it became a private confession amidst the wreckage of the training hall. "I have been developing a workshop."
"Something I have never tested in practical application..."
"Something that operates outside the standard parameters of combat."
Iris’s entire demeanor shifted. The professional detachment wavered.
"What kind of working?"
"The soul register," Rex said.
The words seemed to freeze the air.
"Soul register?" she repeated, her voice scarcely more than a breath.
"Communication with the recently departed," Rex explained, his tone clinical despite the impossibility of the subject. "It isn’t standard magical taxonomy.
"It’s a system granted working a deep layer protocol I discovered while excavating the academy archives."
"The archives indicated the possibility existed, but the theory remained unverified..."
"I have been researching the mechanics of the connection between the physical expiration and the residual soul echo."

"If it works," Rex said, his voice dropping to a register of raw honesty, "I can give you one conversation."
"One single, fleeting exchange with Veylor... Not a resurrection. I am not claiming to play god."

Her face was a mask of controlled agony; her eyes searched his for any sign of deception, any hint of a cruel gambit.
"You cannot promise that it works," she said finally.
It wasn’t an accusation; it was a desperate plea for honesty. "You cannot promise me that the system won’t fail or that the connection won’t be empty."
"No," Rex said, his gaze unflinching. "I cannot promise success."
"But I can promise you this: the research suggests it is possible, and I intend to attempt it regardless of whether you agree to the sparring."
"The pursuit of this knowledge is my objective... The offer to you is simply... a consequence of that pursuit."
Iris closed her eyes for a moment, absorbing the brutal truth of his words. She understood perfectly.
He wasn’t using Veylor as a bargaining chip to force her hand. He wasn’t dangling a carrot to manipulate her into training.
He was describing a terrifying coincidence, two parallel paths that had suddenly, violently, collided.

Her delivery was flat and clinical, possessing the terrifying confidence of someone who had already examined the autopsy reports of history. "I have read documentation of it in the Nightwing household’s restricted archives..."

"The documented success rate in historical cases is approximately sixty percent."

The number sounded like a death sentence.

Iris’s fingers curled into fists at her sides. "What happens in the other forty percent? What is the cost of failure?"

"The soul layer remains silent, and you do not lose anything you have not already lost."
"This is not a work that can shatter what remains of your grief; it can only fail to heal it... It can only fail to make it better.

Rex followed.

Those twelve had been a unit, a well-oiled machine of systematic instruction and coordinated technique. They were soldiers, trained to fight within the lines of a curriculum.
Iris was not a soldier. She was an assassin.

Her skills had not been forged in a classroom but in the desperate, blood-soaked margins of survival, where the only question that mattered was not whether a technique was ’clean’ but whether she would be breathing when the exchange ended.
She lacked the polished, textbook elegance of the others. Instead, she possessed something far more dangerous: a terrifying, adaptive fluidity.
She was fast.

It wasn’t the artificial, augmented speed of a system-enhanced ability; it was something more visceral. It was the honed, contextual speed of a predator that had spent years solving the singular problem of closing distance against targets who wanted her dead.
Her movement wasn’t linear; it was a series of lethal geometries.

She exploded toward him, but not from a direct approach. The floor’s geometry suggested a straight line, but Iris defied it. Her body lurched right, a feint that suggested a wide arc, before her momentum snapped left with bone-jarring force.
Rex’s Foresight screamed a warning: ’Imminent engagement in 6 seconds.’
His body reacted before her muscles had even fully committed to the strike.
He let the first exchange play out as naturally as possible, testing the waters of her lethality.
Iris fought with a calibrated, deadly intent. She lacked the frantic urgency of the desperate; she fought with the cold efficiency of someone who was deliberately preserving her options.
Every strike was a question: How do you respond to this? How fast are your reflexes here? Where is the crack in your armor?
She was probing his defenses not to break them yet but to map them. She was learning from him through violence.
And Rex was learning her.
His martial arts mastery already contained every technique Iris could possibly execute; he knew the ’how’ of her movements. What he was doing now was learning the ’why.’

He was cataloging the minute tells that no textbook could teach: the way she shifted her weight onto her left foot milliseconds before a direction change; the specific, minute tension in her jaw that signaled a maximum commitment strike; the way her pupils dilated when she spotted what she believed was an opening.

He wasn’t just fighting an opponent; he was downloading a blueprint of a killer. Every twitch, every microexpression, every heartbeat was being filed away into his consciousness, turning her into a known variable in his ever-expanding equation of war.

chapters.title: Chapter 898. That Handshake Was A Trap, I Should’ve Seen It Coming, (I Did)
paragraphs: The engagement stretched far beyond the brief, brutal massacre of the twelve fighters. What had been a demonstration of dominance had transformed into a grinding, intimate war of attrition.

Minute after agonizing minute, Iris circled Rex like a wolf assessing a mountain, probing his defenses with strikes that carried the venom of experience. She tested angles that no trained unit fighter would ever conceive, angles born not from textbooks but from the desperate necessity of finding a gap when the only alternative was a corpse in the dirt.
She lunged.
It was a low, compressed entry that Rex had never seen from the twelve. She didn’t just move; she seemed to collapse toward the floor, her body becoming a projectile that skimmed the hardwood.
The movement was grotesquely efficient, designed to exploit the blind spot beneath a fighter’s peripheral vision. Rex had to burn through his reserves to intercept it.
His elbow connected with her shoulder with a wet, meaty thud, forcing her to abort the strike, but the effort left him breathing harder than he had all morning.
His mind raced: ’This isn’t technique... This is survival instinct rendered as motion.’
Thirty seconds later, she struck again. Same compressed low entry, but from a completely different vector.
This time, Rex was ready. He caught her wrist mid-lunge, his grip tightening like a vice.

The sound of her tendons straining under his pressure echoed in the silent hall. He deflected the attack with a brutal efficiency that left her stumbling, but he felt the sting of her adaptation; she had already adjusted the timing of her second attempt based on his reaction to the first.
She adjusted a third time, her movements becoming more erratic, more dangerous.
"She learns fast," Aurelia murmured from the hall’s edge, her voice carrying a rare note of genuine fascination.
She didn’t look away from the violence unfolding. "Faster than the unit did."
"That is the specific advantage of training that was never systematic... Nothing about her combat language is inherited from anyone else’s assumptions."
"That is one way of describing years of surviving alone," Elaris replied, her tone laced with a bitter understanding. "Training in the absence of teachers."
"It is not a kind way to describe it," Aurelia corrected coldly. "But it is an accurate one."
Aurelia’s voice cut through the tension twice more, calling out commands not to Rex but to Iris. Each call was a provocation, a challenge to abandon caution and commit fully to the kill.

Each time, Iris responded with a visible shift in her combat posture, a sudden increase in aggression, and a willingness to sacrifice defense for lethal momentum. Rex saw the shift coming before her muscles even twitched; he read the intent in the way her center of gravity dropped.
The climax arrived exactly when Rex’s calculations predicted.

Iris had been building momentum for thirty seconds, weaving a complex tapestry of feints and strikes that drew Rex into a specific pocket of space. It was a trap designed to force him into close quarters, setting up the final element: a high-level assassin’s throw.
Rex waited. He saw the trap closing.
The first phase of the throw began with the grip. Iris’s fingers locked onto his arm with the desperate strength of a drowning person.
She found his leverage points with terrifying accuracy, her nails digging into his skin as she prepared to wrench his balance from under him.
Rex didn’t fight the grip. He embraced it.

The moment her leverage reached its peak, Rex moved not against the force of the throw, but with it. He twisted his entire body at the exact point of her leverage, turning her own mechanical advantage into a weapon against her.
The physics of the counterthrow were absolute.
Iris was airborne for a heartbeat before she slammed into the hardwood. The impact was sickening; the sound of her body hitting the floor was less of a slap and more of a bone-deep crunch.
The air rushed out of her lungs in a strangled gasp as her ribs groaned under the sudden deceleration.
But she was an assassin.
Two seconds after impact, her muscles spasmed and she rolled, forcing herself back onto her feet with a ragged, desperate energy. But then she stopped.
Her legs buckled slightly, and she sank back down to a seated position.
Her body had processed the trauma. The damage was real: the shockwave of the landing had reverberated through her spine, and her nervous system was screaming warnings.
Her mind was already running the grim calculus of the assassin: ’Am I broken? Can I stand again, or am I already dead?’
She needed thirty seconds, thirty seconds of agonizing stillness, to assess whether continuing the fight was a viable option or a suicide mission.
Blood trickled from a split cuticle where she had gripped him, staining the floor. Through the haze of pain and the ringing in her ears, Iris lifted her head.
She looked at Rex from the floor, her eyes raw, bleeding with both physical pain and the terrifying realization that she had finally met something she couldn’t simply outlive.
"That was the longest anyone has held out against you this morning," Iris said. Her voice was rough; each word dragged through a throat tight with pain.

She was breathing in ragged, uneven stabs, her chest heaving as she fought to reoxygenate blood that was pooling in her bruised tissues. Despite the sweat streaming down her face and the tremor in her hands, there was a spark in her eyes, the razor-edged pride of a predator who had been beaten but refused to acknowledge the humiliation of the defeat.
She had made him work. She had forced him out of his textbook perfection and into the mud.
"It was," Rex admitted, his own breathing measured but heavy.
His shirt was torn at the shoulder where her grip had nearly torn the muscle from the bone. "You made me use techniques the unit never required..."
"They fought to win; you fought to survive. That changes the calculus entirely."
Iris stared at him for a heartbeat, the silence in the hall stretching until it felt like it would snap.
"I accept," she said. The words were a vow.
Rex reached down, offering his hand.
For a fraction of a second, Iris stared at his palm. Then, her fingers closed around his, but it wasn’t the grip of someone accepting help.
It was the grip of someone seizing a weapon.
’Now.’

Her entire body coiled like a released spring. She didn’t pull herself up; she launched herself forward, using his outstretched arm as a fulcrum to swing her weight into a vicious, close-quarters headbutt aimed directly at his nose.
The wet crack of bone on bone echoed as she drove her forehead into his face, but Rex had already anticipated the deception.
The moment her fingers touched his skin, his Foresight flashed crimson: ’Deception detected. Counterstrike imminent.’
Instead of pulling away, Rex snapped his free hand upward in a brutal rising elbow.
THWACK.
The strike caught her just below the jawline as she came in. Iris’s head snapped back, blood spraying from her split lip in a fine crimson mist.
She didn’t retreat; she couldn’t afford to. Instead, she twisted mid-air, turning the momentum of the blow into a spinning back kick aimed at Rex’s solar plexus.
Oof!
Rex caught the kick with both forearms, the impact sending a shockwave through his bones that felt like being hit by a sledgehammer.
CRACK.
The sound of his own tendons straining under the force filled his ears.
"Still learning?" Rex gritted out through clenched teeth, his muscles bulging as he fought to hold her leg in place.
"Still fighting," Iris hissed.
She didn’t wait for him to release her. She brought her free knee up with terrifying speed, aiming for his ribs.
CRUNCH.
The sound of ribs protesting the impact was sickening. Rex gasped, the air leaving his lungs in a pained wheeze, but he didn’t break his hold.
He redirected her momentum, twisting his torso to slam her sideways into the nearest pillar.
BOOM.
The impact against the stone column knocked the wind out of her completely. Iris slumped for a microsecond, blood streaming from her nose and mouth, painting her chin crimson.
But before she could slide to the floor, she drove an elbow backward into Rex’s sternum THUD and spun around, claws extended like she intended to tear flesh from bone.
She was a whirlwind of desperate, ugly violence. She slashed at his eyes, aimed for his throat, and threw herself at his knees.
Each attack was followed by a countermove that defied conventional physics: a palm strike to the throat, a fingernail rake across a forearm, a vicious knee to the thigh.
Rex met her with the cold precision of a surgeon. He moved through her storm of strikes with terrifying economy.
When she lunged with a throat strike, he parried with a forearm that sounded like two planks of wood colliding CLACK and followed immediately with a devastating liver shot.
Splat.
Iris doubled over, a strangled cry escaping her lips as the pain radiated through her entire torso. But even as she bent, she attempted to sweep Rex’s legs.
He jumped the sweep, but she anticipated the leap, rising from her crouch to catch him midair with a desperate, two-handed grab to his throat.

When she lunged with a throat strike, he parried with a forearm that sounded like two planks of wood colliding CLACK and followed immediately with a devastating liver shot.
Splat.
Iris doubled over, a strangled cry escaping her lips as the pain radiated through her entire torso.
But even as she bent, she attempted to sweep Rex’s legs.
He jumped the sweep, but she anticipated the leap, rising from her crouch to catch him midair with a desperate, two-handed grab to his throat.

chapters.title: Chapter 899. Power Isn’t A Gift, It’s A Conquest, Very Marketable Slogan
paragraphs: They crashed to the ground together, a tangle of limbs, blood, and labored breathing. They rolled across the blood-slicked floor, each trying to position themselves for a killing blow.

Rex managed to pin her wrist against the hardwood, his forearm pressing down on her throat with enough pressure to bruise, while Iris had her fingers hooked like talons around the tendons of his inner elbow.
The hall was silent save for their ragged, animalistic panting. Blood from both of them smeared the floor where they struggled, creating a grotesque tableau of crimson streaks.
Rex looked down at her, his vision swimming with adrenaline and pain. Iris looked up at him, her face a mask of blood and sweat, her eyes burning with a terrifying, beautiful ferocity.
"You’re not... done," she whispered, the words bubbling through the blood in her mouth.

The violence in the center of the room died not because the combatants chose to stop but because the very atmosphere of the hall shifted. The air grew heavy, charged with a different kind of pressure, not the chaotic, adrenaline-fueled pressure of a fight, but the crushing, absolute weight of sovereignty.
Aurelia stepped onto the training floor.
Her movement was precise, each footfall carrying the undeniable authority of the woman who owned the ground beneath them. She moved like a queen entering a battlefield she had already won.
The twelve fighters, their bodies bruised and bloodied from Rex’s earlier rampage, scrambled to find some semblance of dignity, straightening their backs despite their injuries.

Diana, standing at the hall’s edge, went deathly still, her breathing catching in her throat. Elaris opened her mouth as if to protest or interject, but the look in Aurelia’s eyes froze the words before they could form.
Aurelia didn’t look at the wounded; she looked at the survivors. Her gaze swept over the assembled family, the guards, and the broken bodies on the floor.

"Rex Rexilion has defeated twelve of this household’s elite unit without invoking a single system ability," she began, her voice carrying to every corner of the vaulted ceiling like a tolling bell. "He engaged Iris, an assassin who survived on instinct alone, and neutralized her in less than three minutes of sustained combat."
She paused, letting the implications sink in. The silence was deafening.

"What you have witnessed in this hour is not the performance of a man who succeeded through fortune or exceptional circumstances," she continued, her eyes locking onto Rex’s with unsettling intensity. "What you have seen is a predator whose capabilities exceed nearly everything this household has ever produced."

A cold shiver seemed to ripple through the remaining guards. The Nightwing household was built on a foundation of superiority, a legacy forged in blood and maintained through generations of absolute dominance.

"The Nightwing household has maintained its position in Aethelgard for four generations through one singular commitment," Aurelia said, her voice hardening. "We produce fighters who are objectively better than those who seek to replace us."
"My husband is currently on an extended mission, and during his absence, this household’s military capacity has been managed through the existing unit structure."
"But the unit structure has proven insufficient."
She turned fully toward Rex, her silhouette sharp against the torchlight.
"I am offering you the position of acting combat director for this household’s training program," she stated. "This authority is temporary, valid only until my husband’s return."
"But the mandate is absolute: you will improve this unit... You will raise them to a standard that matches our name.

The twelve fighters exchanged glances, some filled with resentment, others with a dawning, terrified respect. The idea of a stranger, a man who had just dismantled them like marionettes, commanding their training was a bitter pill to swallow.
Aurelia’s lips curled into something that wasn’t quite a smile but lacked any warmth.
"However," she added, her voice dropping to a dangerous, intimate register. "Power must be validated and authority must be earned through more than just words."
She stepped closer to Rex, crossing the invisible line that separated the instructor from the student. The tension in the room spiked to a breaking point.
"Before we discuss contracts and mandates, I have one question, Rex Rexilion." Her eyes searched his, challenging every fiber of his being. "Strip away the systems. Strip away the enhancements."
"If we were to stand here, right now, in a fair fight—no abilities, no magic, no tricks, just two bodies, two sets of hands and feet in a raw, primal brawl... could you beat me?"
The question hung in the air like a guillotine blade. She wasn’t asking for a demonstration; she was offering a test of fundamental truth.
Rex didn’t flinch. He didn’t even blink.
He stood amidst the bloodstains and the broken bodies of the elite unit, his chest rising and falling in a slow, controlled rhythm that betrayed none of the carnage he had just endured.

"You want to talk about validation?" Rex asked, his voice carrying a gravelly resonance that seemed to vibrate in the very bones of those listening. "You want to know if I can back up the claim of authority?"
A slow, dangerous smile spread across his face. "I will accept your position, Aurelia."
"I will take your mandate. But I won’t take it as some hired hand who simply follows orders..."
"I will take it because I believe in the necessity of what must be done."

He turned his head to survey the room, the resentful fighters, the stunned guards, and the silent family members. "If you want me to improve this household, then you must understand something fundamental about strength."
"Strength isn’t something you inherit through a family name."
"It isn’t something you preserve in a textbook or protect behind a system ability."
"Strength is a living thing. It is something that must be hunted, something that must be bled for, something that must be taken from the world through sheer, unrelenting will.
His eyes burned with a fervor that made several of the guards step back. "I will fight every single person in this room if I have to."
"I will break every bone, bruise every muscle, and shatter every assumption until only the truth remains: either you are strong enough to survive, or you are not."
"If you want me to lead them, I will not teach them how to follow... I will teach them how to dominate."
He turned his attention back to Aurelia, the intensity of his gaze locking onto hers like a physical weight. "Power isn’t a gift, Aurelia. It’s a conquest."
Aurelia watched him, her expression unreadable. She had spent her life surrounded by nobles who spoke of power in whispers and politics, men who wore their authority like expensive silk.
But this man, this man, spoke of power like a butcher speaks of meat, raw and undeniable. For the first time in years, something unfamiliar stirred beneath her composure.
Something primal. Something that recognized its equal.
A sound escaped her throat, a soft chuckle that quickly escalated into a rich, genuine laugh that echoed off the vaulted stone ceiling. It was a sound of pure, exhilarated recognition.
"You speak like a man who has already burned down the world to build something better," she said, her laughter dying down into a hungry grin.
She began to move, but not toward him. She circled, her movements fluid and deceptively casual, as she shed the mantle of the noble matriarch.
"Very well, Rex Rexilion. Let us test the foundation of your philosophy."
She dropped into a fighting stance. It wasn’t the polished, practiced stance of a duelist; it was something older, something more dangerous.
Her center of gravity was low, her hands open and relaxed, fingertips twitching like a cat preparing to spring. The air around her seemed to tighten.
Rex mirrored her, stepping into his own stance, compact, coiled, and utterly lethal. The muscles in his shoulders bunched, his eyes narrowing as he entered the hyperfocused state of the predator.
"One warning, Aurelia," Rex said, his voice dropping to a deadly murmur. "If I win, if I prove that my philosophy holds true... do not regret it when everything in this household starts changing."
"Do not regret it when I tear down the old ways to make room for the new. Because once I start, I won’t stop until the transformation is complete."
Aurelia’s eyes flashed with defiance, a challenge that burned brighter than any torch in the hall. "Regret? You mistake me for one of these children, Rex."
"I didn’t survive four generations of Nightwing politics by fearing change." She beckoned him forward with a flick of her wrist, her stance shifting to something even more aggressive. "Come then."
"Show me this ’conquest’ you speak of..."
"Show me if you are truly the storm you claim to be or if you’re just another gust of wind passing through my halls."

chapters.title: Chapter 900. Two Armored Vehicles Crashing At Full Speed, Also Just Us
paragraphs: The air between them didn’t just tense; it ignited. For three heartbeats, the entire hall held its breath, a vacuum of silence where the only sound was the distant crackle of torches.
Then, Rex exploded forward.
He didn’t rush; he launched. His first strike was a piston-like straight right aimed directly at Aurelia’s sternum, designed to wind her before she could react.
Aurelia didn’t retreat. Instead, she pivoted on the ball of her left foot, her body spinning with the grace of a dancer and the lethal intent of a viper.
Rex’s fist cut through empty air with a vicious whoosh, and in that same microsecond, Aurelia unleashed a roundhouse kick aimed at his temple.
WHIP CRACK.

Rex ducked, the wind of her shin passing inches above his scalp. He immediately drove his shoulder into her midsection, attempting to drive her backward, but Aurelia was like water; she flowed around his impact.
She grabbed his extended arm, used his momentum against him, and attempted to twist his elbow into a break.
GRIND.

Rex roared, a sound of pure animal defiance, as he braced his forearm against his own bicep to prevent the joint from snapping. He twisted his hips violently, breaking her grip, and countered with a devastating knee strike aimed at her ribs.
THUD.
Aurelia caught the knee with both palms, the impact sending a visible shockwave through her shoulders. Her feet skidded across the hardwood, leaving faint scorch marks from the sheer friction.
"Not bad," she hissed through gritted teeth, her eyes blazing. "But you’re telegraphing your intent with that anger, Rex!"
She lunged. This wasn’t a probe; it was a barrage.
A left hook, a spinning elbow, and a lightning-fast jab that forced Rex into a desperate defensive shell. Rex retreated two steps, his forearms raised in a cross block.
CLACK CLACK CLACK.
Each impact sounded like two sledgehammers colliding. His bones vibrated with each blow, the sting of her precision strikes seeping through his guard.
He saw her opening, a split-second hesitation after her jab, and he seized it. Rex stepped inside her guard, abandoning defense for raw, crushing offense.
He delivered a three-punch combination: a left uppercut that snapped her head back, a right hook that caught her jaw, and a brutal left cross to the solar plexus.
CRACK. THWACK. OOF.

Aurelia gasped as the air was punched from her lungs, but she refused to collapse. Instead, she grabbed Rex’s collar, pulling him closer as she drove her forehead into his nose with a sickening CRUNCH.
Blood erupted from Rex’s nose, spraying across both their faces. The pain was white hot, a searing lightning bolt that momentarily clouded his vision.
But the pain only served to sharpen his focus. The world narrowed down to the taste of copper in his mouth and the heat of Aurelia’s body pressed against his.
They entered a state of pure, unadulterated violence, a close-quarters brawl where technique blurred into primal instinct. They traded blows with terrifying frequency.
Rex landed a heavy kick to her thigh that sounded like a wet branch breaking; Aurelia responded with a palm strike to his ear that sent his equilibrium spinning.
BAM. WHACK. CRUNCH.
Rex grabbed her wrist, attempting to execute a bone-breaking twist, but Aurelia dropped her weight instantly, becoming impossibly heavy.
She drove her forehead into his chest and spun, catching Rex in a leg sweep that sent him crashing to one knee. Before he could recover, she was on him, her fists raining down like hammer blows.
THUD. THUD. THUD.
Rex rolled backward, the floorboards splintering under the force of his escape. He came up swinging, a wild, sweeping kick that caught her mid-torso.
Aurelia flew backward several feet, her boots skidding across the blood-slicked floor, but she landed in a crouch, already coiled for the next assault.
Both were drenched in sweat and crimson. Their breathing was no longer human; it was the ragged, desperate gasping of two apex predators fighting for dominance.

Blood dripped from Rex’s chin onto the floor, mixing with the stains already there. Aurelia’s lip was split badly, a steady stream of red running down her chin, but her eyes remained fixed on him with terrifying clarity.
"Is this..." Aurelia panted, wiping blood from her eye with the back of her hand, "...is this the ’conquest’ you promised?"
Rex wiped his nose, smearing more blood across his cheek. His muscles screamed, and his ribs felt like they were grinding together, but a savage grin split his face.
"We haven’t even started breaking things yet, Aurelia."

He charged again, not with a technique, but with the unstoppable force of a landslide, his fists clenched and his eyes locked on hers. The clash that followed was louder, more brutal, and more desperate than anything the Nightwing household had witnessed in centuries.

The collision between them sounded less like human combat and more like two armored vehicles crashing at full speed. When Rex met Aurelia’s charge, the force of their impact sent a shockwave through the training floor that made the nearby guards stumble.
Rex threw a devastating haymaker, a right hook that carried the weight of his entire body behind it. But Aurelia didn’t just dodge; she danced through the danger zone.

She dipped her shoulder beneath his arm, the motion so fluid it seemed almost supernatural, and as she passed inside his guard, she unleashed a devastating combo that demonstrated why she was the matriarch of this bloodline.
WHIP THUD CRACK!

First came a lightning-fast left palm strike to Rex’s diaphragm, forcing the air from his lungs in a wet wheeze. Before he could recover his breath, she spun on her heel, converting the momentum into a vicious elbow strike that caught Rex squarely across the cheekbone.
CRACK.

The sound of cartilage protesting echoed off the stone walls. Without pausing for even a heartbeat, Aurelia followed through with a snap kick to his kneecap, her shin connecting with the joint with the force of a breaking sledgehammer.
THWACK.
Rex grunted as his leg buckled, but his training took over. Instead of falling, he used the pain as fuel.
As Aurelia pulled back to reset, Rex twisted his torso mid-collapse, driving an uppercut upward that caught her under the chin.
BOOM.
Aurelia’s head snapped back violently, blood spraying from her mouth as her teeth collided. She stumbled backward, but Rex was already on her.

He lunged forward like a wounded bull, his fists becoming a blur of relentless aggression. He threw a left jab to her eyes to obscure her vision, followed immediately by a thunderous right cross to her ribs.
PUFF. CRUNCH.
Aurelia gasped as a rib visibly shifted under the impact, but her fury only intensified.
"Is that all?" she roared through the blood.

She met his aggression with a counter combo that left the onlookers speechless. As Rex swung for a finishing blow, Aurelia caught his wrist with both hands, twisting her body sideways to redirect his power into the floor.
While he was off balance, she drove two consecutive knee strikes into his solar plexus, THUD THUD, each one more precise than the last, designed to collapse his diaphragm.
Rex staggered, his vision swimming with dark spots, but as she moved in to capitalize, he threw his forehead forward in a brutal headbutt.
CRUNCH.

The sound of their skulls colliding was sickening. Both fighters recoiled, blood streaming down their foreheads. Rex’s nose was a ruin of broken cartilage, and Aurelia’s left eye began to swell shut instantly.
They stood three feet apart for a moment, both swaying, their breathing coming in ragged, desperate gasps that sounded like tearing cloth.
"You... fight like a demon," Aurelia spat, wiping a thick smear of blood from her lips.
Her voice was thick, her composure shattered, replaced by something far more dangerous: genuine bloodlust.
"And you..." Rex growled, spitting a glob of crimson onto the floor, "...fight like you were born from a massacre."
Rex charged again, but this time it was different. He wasn’t just throwing strikes; he was weaving them together.

He feinted a high kick, drawing Aurelia’s guard up, then immediately dropped low, driving a vicious leg sweep that caught her ankles. As she stumbled, he came up with a rising elbow aimed at her throat.
WHOOSH.
Aurelia twisted her neck at the last millisecond, the elbow grazing her carotid artery. She retaliated with a spinning back fist that caught Rex across the temple.
WHACK.
His head snapped sideways, blood spurting from a fresh gash on his scalp.
The fight descended into a beautiful, horrifying chaos. They became two storms colliding in the center of the hall.
Rex would land a crushing blow to her ribs (THUD), and Aurelia would respond with a flurry of three precise punches to his kidney and liver (BAM BAM BAM), forcing him to double over.
When he would grab her, attempting to crush her throat with his forearm, she would drive her thumbs into his pressure points, seeking to paralyze his grip.
GRIND. SNAP. THUD.
The floor beneath them was no longer wood; it was a slick, crimson mire of sweat and blood. Every time they landed a solid hit, the sound reverberated through the room like a gunshot.
The elite unit watched in stunned silence, recognizing that they weren’t watching a spar; they were watching two gods tearing each other apart to see who would claim the throne.
Rex’s knuckles were split open, dripping blood onto Aurelia’s torn training gear. Aurelia’s breathing was a series of broken sobs of exertion, her ribs bruised to the bone.
Yet neither would yield. Each time one stumbled, the other would press the advantage with renewed ferocity, their movements becoming more primal, less technical, and infinitely more deadly.
